cards.q: In the length tension relationship, what sets the amount of active tension a sarcomere can generate at a given length?
cards.a: The number of myosin heads that can reach binding sites on actin.
options: The number of myosin heads that can reach binding sites on actin
The amount of ATP stored inside the sarcomere
The resting membrane potential of the muscle fiber
The length of the thick filament itself
cards.explanation: Active tension tracks the overlap between thick and thin filaments, because overlap decides how many crossbridges can form, and each crossbridge adds a fixed increment of force. Stored ATP is not limiting in a rested fiber, so it does not shape the curve. Resting membrane potential decides whether the fiber fires at all, not how much force one contraction produces. Thick filament length is fixed near 1.6 micrometers and does not change when the sarcomere is stretched.

cards.q: At about what sarcomere length does a skeletal muscle fiber generate its maximal active tension?
cards.a: About 2.0 to 2.2 micrometers.
options: About 1.2 to 1.4 micrometers
About 3.0 to 3.2 micrometers
About 2.0 to 2.2 micrometers
About 3.6 to 3.8 micrometers
cards.explanation: Optimal length sits near 2.0 to 2.2 micrometers, where every myosin head in the crossbridge bearing region lies opposite a thin filament. At 1.2 to 1.4 micrometers the thick filaments are already jammed against the Z discs. At 3.0 to 3.2 micrometers overlap is partial and tension is on the descending limb. At 3.6 micrometers and beyond the filaments have pulled apart completely and active tension is zero.

cards.q: Passive tension in a stretched skeletal muscle comes mainly from which source?
cards.a: Titin and the connective tissue surrounding the fibers.
options: Titin and the connective tissue surrounding the fibers
Crossbridges cycling slowly without Ca2+
Ca2+ still bound to troponin C
The Na+/K+ ATPase holding the fiber polarized
cards.explanation: Passive tension is elastic recoil, and it comes from titin inside the sarcomere plus the collagen of endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium outside it. It appears in a relaxed, unstimulated muscle, so cycling crossbridges cannot be the source. Ca2+ bound to troponin would produce active tension, not passive. The Na+/K+ ATPase maintains ion gradients and has no mechanical role in resisting stretch.

cards.q: On the descending limb of the length tension curve, what has changed compared with the plateau?
cards.a: Overlap between thick and thin filaments has decreased.
options: Thick filaments have buckled against the Z discs
Thin filaments from the two ends now overlap each other
Overlap between thick and thin filaments has decreased
Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum has stopped
cards.explanation: Pulling the sarcomere past optimal length slides the thin filaments away from the myosin heads, so fewer crossbridges can form and tension falls in direct proportion to the lost overlap. Buckling of thick filaments against the Z discs and double overlap of thin filaments both happen at short lengths, on the ascending limb, not the descending limb. Ca2+ release is unchanged; the deficit is mechanical, not a failure of excitation contraction coupling.

cards.q: Total tension recorded from a muscle at a given length is the sum of which two components?
cards.a: Active tension plus passive tension.
options: Isometric tension plus isotonic tension
Active tension plus passive tension
Twitch tension plus tetanic tension
Series elastic tension minus parallel elastic tension
cards.explanation: Total tension is what the transducer reads, and it combines the crossbridge derived active tension with the elastic passive tension already present before stimulation. Isometric and isotonic name conditions of contraction, not components that add together. Twitch and tetanic tension are two ways of stimulating the same muscle, so they are alternatives rather than addends. Series and parallel elastic elements both contribute to passive tension, and they are not subtracted from one another.

cards.q: At very short sarcomere lengths, what physically limits the tension a fiber can produce?
cards.a: Thick filaments hit the Z discs and thin filaments overlap each other.
options: Thick and thin filaments have lost all overlap
Titin has been stretched past its elastic limit
Thick filaments hit the Z discs and thin filaments overlap each other
Troponin can no longer bind the Ca2+ released during the twitch
cards.explanation: Squeezing the sarcomere below about 2.0 micrometers forces the thin filaments from opposite ends past each other and drives the rigid thick filaments into the Z discs, both of which oppose further shortening. Complete loss of overlap is the opposite problem and belongs at very long lengths. Titin is slack at short lengths, not overstretched. Troponin binds Ca2+ normally, so the loss of force is mechanical rather than a signaling failure.

cards.q: What structural feature of the thick filament explains the flat plateau at the top of the length tension curve?
cards.a: The central bare zone carries no myosin heads.
options: The central bare zone carries no myosin heads
The Z discs stretch elastically over a short range
Titin unfolds at constant tension over that range
The T tubules reach their widest diameter over that range
cards.explanation: Across the plateau the thin filaments slide over the bare zone, a stretch of thick filament with no heads on it, so the number of crossbridges that can form does not change and tension stays flat. Z discs are anchoring structures and do not stretch enough to flatten the curve. Titin does unfold under load, but that shapes passive tension at long lengths rather than the active plateau. T tubule diameter has no bearing on filament overlap.

cards.q: Where on the length tension curve does an intact skeletal muscle normally rest in the body?
cards.a: At or very close to optimal length.
options: Far out on the descending limb
Well down the ascending limb
At or very close to optimal length
Past the point where active tension reaches zero
cards.explanation: Tendon attachments and joint anatomy hold most skeletal muscles near optimal length at rest, so ordinary movements start close to peak force. Sitting far out on the descending limb would waste most of the muscle's force capacity. Sitting well down the ascending limb would do the same at the other extreme. No intact muscle rests past the point of zero overlap, since the joint would have to be dislocated to get there.

cards.q: A single sarcomere is stretched to 3.7 micrometers, beyond the point where thick and thin filaments overlap at all, and then stimulated. Predict its active tension.
cards.a: Essentially zero, because no crossbridges can form.
options: About half of maximum, because half the heads still reach actin
Maximal, because the filaments are fully extended
Essentially zero, because no crossbridges can form
Above maximal, because elastic recoil adds to crossbridge force
cards.explanation: Active tension is proportional to overlap, and at 3.7 micrometers the thin filaments have slid clear of every myosin head, so no crossbridge can attach and active tension collapses to zero. Half maximal tension would require partial overlap, which is what you see closer to 3.0 micrometers. Stretch does not improve crossbridge access; it removes it. Elastic recoil at this length is real and large, but it is passive tension, and passive tension is measured separately from active tension.

cards.q: A fiber is held at a sarcomere length of 1.6 micrometers and stimulated. Compared with the same fiber at 2.1 micrometers, what happens to active tension and why?
cards.a: Lower, because thick filaments are compressed against the Z discs.
options: Lower, because thick and thin filaments no longer overlap
Lower, because thick filaments are compressed against the Z discs
Higher, because more crossbridges can form at short lengths
Unchanged, because the number of crossbridges is fixed
cards.explanation: At 1.6 micrometers the sarcomere is on the ascending limb, where the thick filaments run into the Z discs and the thin filaments interfere with each other, so force is well below the value at 2.1 micrometers. Loss of overlap is the right idea for the wrong limb; that explains the fall at long lengths. Shortening does not add crossbridges, because the extra sliding happens over the bare zone. Crossbridge number is exactly what changes with length, which is the whole point of the curve.

cards.q: A relaxed muscle is stretched progressively beyond its optimal length. Predict what happens to passive tension.
cards.a: It rises steeply as the muscle is stretched further.
options: It falls toward zero as the filaments separate
It stays flat until active tension reaches zero
It rises steeply as the muscle is stretched further
It rises briefly and then returns to zero
cards.explanation: Titin and the surrounding connective tissue behave like nonlinear springs, so passive tension is near zero around resting length and then climbs steeply the further the muscle is stretched. It cannot fall as the muscle lengthens, since that is the direction that loads the elastic elements. It does not wait for active tension to disappear before rising; the two curves overlap across a wide range of lengths. And elastic recoil does not release on its own while the stretch is maintained.

cards.q: A person holds the wrist in full flexion, which shortens the finger flexor muscles. Predict the effect on maximum grip force and the reason for it.
cards.a: Grip force falls, because the flexor sarcomeres now sit below optimal length.
options: Grip force rises, because the muscle is already partly shortened
Grip force is unchanged, because force depends only on motor unit recruitment
Grip force falls, because the flexor sarcomeres now sit below optimal length
Grip force falls, because filament overlap is completely lost
cards.explanation: Flexing the wrist slackens the finger flexors onto the ascending limb, where thick filaments crowd the Z discs, so the same maximal effort produces less force. A partly shortened muscle is weaker, not stronger, once it passes optimal length. Recruitment does set force, but the force each recruited fiber can make still depends on its length. Total loss of overlap describes the far end of the descending limb, which is the opposite of what wrist flexion does.

cards.q: Two sarcomeres in the same fiber are compared, one at 2.2 micrometers and one at 2.8 micrometers. Which generates more active tension, and why?
cards.a: The 2.2 micrometer sarcomere, because more myosin heads lie opposite thin filaments.
options: The 2.8 micrometer sarcomere, because it has more distance available to shorten
The 2.8 micrometer sarcomere, because passive tension adds to crossbridge force
They are equal, because both lie on the plateau of the curve
The 2.2 micrometer sarcomere, because more myosin heads lie opposite thin filaments
cards.explanation: At 2.2 micrometers the sarcomere is at the top of the plateau, while 2.8 micrometers is out on the descending limb with reduced overlap, so the shorter one forms more crossbridges and makes more active force. Available shortening distance does not determine peak tension, which is measured isometrically. Passive tension is a separate component and is not counted as active tension. The plateau ends near 2.2 micrometers, so the two lengths are not equivalent.

cards.q: Why does shortening a sarcomere from 2.2 to 2.0 micrometers fail to increase active tension?
cards.a: The extra sliding crosses the bare zone, which has no myosin heads.
options: The extra sliding crosses the bare zone, which has no myosin heads
Ca2+ release falls as the sarcomere shortens
Titin begins to resist any further shortening
Thin filaments begin to detach from the Z discs at very short lengths
cards.explanation: Between roughly 2.0 and 2.2 micrometers the thin filaments advance over the head free bare zone, so no new crossbridges are gained and tension holds flat. Ca2+ release is set by the action potential, not by length over this range. Titin is slack rather than resistive at lengths at or below optimal. Thin filaments stay anchored to the Z discs throughout, which is what allows them to transmit force at all.

cards.q: A whole muscle stretched well beyond optimal length shows a higher total tension than at optimal length, even though its active tension is lower. What explains this?
cards.a: Passive tension from titin and connective tissue is large at long lengths.
options: Passive tension from titin and connective tissue is large at long lengths
Crossbridge cycling speeds up when the muscle is stretched
The muscle recruits extra motor units when it is stretched
Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum increases with stretch
cards.explanation: Total tension is active plus passive, and at long lengths the steeply rising passive component more than makes up for the crossbridges lost to poor overlap. Crossbridge cycling rate sets shortening velocity, not the height of an isometric plateau, and stretch does not speed it. Recruitment is a nervous system decision and is not triggered by passively stretching the muscle. Ca2+ release is essentially unchanged, which is why active tension falls rather than rises.

cards.q: A muscle is tested isometrically at four lengths. Length A: total tension 100, passive 0. Length B: total 110, passive 20. Length C: total 120, passive 60. Length D: total 70, passive 0. Which length is closest to the optimal length for active tension?
cards.a: Length A.
options: Length B
Length C
Length D
Length A
cards.explanation: Subtract passive from total to get active tension: A gives 100, B gives 90, C gives 60, and D gives 70, so A produces the most crossbridge force and sits closest to optimal length. Length C is the trap, because its total tension is the highest recorded, but most of that is elastic recoil rather than crossbridge force. Length B is already onto the descending limb, with passive tension starting to appear. Length D has no passive tension at all, which marks it as a short length on the ascending limb.

cards.q: An elbow is immobilized in a flexed cast for eight weeks. The biceps adapts by removing sarcomeres in series so that its remaining sarcomeres sit near optimal length in the flexed position. Predict what happens when the cast is removed and the elbow is straightened.
cards.a: Active tension falls and passive tension rises, because the shortened muscle is pulled onto its descending limb.
options: Active tension rises and passive tension falls, because the muscle is now closer to optimal length
Active tension falls and passive tension falls, because the sarcomeres are compressed against the Z discs
Active tension falls and passive tension rises, because the shortened muscle is pulled onto its descending limb
Active and passive tension are both unchanged, because sarcomere number does not affect force
cards.explanation: With fewer sarcomeres spanning the same tendon to tendon distance, each remaining sarcomere must stretch further to allow full extension, which pushes it past optimal overlap and loads titin heavily. The muscle is worse off at extension, not better, since optimal length has been reset to the flexed position. Compression against the Z discs is an ascending limb event, and it would not raise passive tension. Sarcomere number in series is precisely what sets the joint angle at which peak force occurs.

cards.q: Grip force is measured at three wrist positions: 20 kg with the wrist fully flexed, 45 kg with the wrist slightly extended, and 30 kg with the wrist fully extended. What best accounts for the pattern?
cards.a: The finger flexors are below optimal length in wrist flexion and beyond optimal length in full extension.
options: The finger flexors are beyond optimal length in wrist flexion and below optimal length in full extension
The finger flexors are below optimal length in wrist flexion and beyond optimal length in full extension
Motor unit recruitment is maximal only in slight extension and submaximal at the two extremes
Passive tension in the finger flexors subtracts from grip force at both extremes of wrist position
cards.explanation: Wrist flexion slackens the finger flexors onto the ascending limb and full wrist extension stretches them onto the descending limb, so both extremes lose crossbridge overlap and peak force appears in between. The reversed version has the limbs backward: flexing a wrist shortens its flexors, it does not lengthen them. Recruitment is under voluntary control and a motivated subject recruits fully at every position tested. Passive tension adds to recorded tension rather than subtracting from it.

cards.q: A stimulated muscle fiber produces 45 units of passive tension and no active tension at all, and the fiber is confirmed to depolarize and release Ca2+ normally. What can you conclude about its sarcomere length?
cards.a: It is stretched past roughly 3.6 micrometers, so thick and thin filaments no longer overlap.
options: It is compressed below roughly 1.3 micrometers, so the thick filaments are crushed against the Z discs
It is stretched past roughly 3.6 micrometers, so thick and thin filaments no longer overlap
It is at optimal length, but the crossbridges have run out of ATP
It is on the plateau, but the Ca2+ signal is too brief to activate troponin
cards.explanation: Normal excitation and Ca2+ release rule out a signaling problem, and the large passive tension tells you the elastic elements are heavily loaded, which only happens at long lengths, so the fiber must be stretched past the point of zero overlap. A crushed short sarcomere would give little or no passive tension, since titin is slack there. Running out of ATP would cause rigor and stiffness, not a clean loss of active force with normal Ca2+ handling. The stem states Ca2+ release is normal, so a defective Ca2+ signal is excluded.

cards.q: What defines an isometric contraction?
cards.a: The muscle develops tension but its length does not change.
options: The muscle shortens while tension stays constant
The muscle lengthens while tension stays constant
The muscle changes length without developing tension
The muscle develops tension but its length does not change
cards.explanation: Isometric means same length: crossbridges cycle and tension climbs, but the load is too large to move, so the muscle holds its length. Shortening at constant tension is a concentric isotonic contraction. Lengthening at constant tension is an eccentric contraction. A length change without tension is not a contraction at all; it is passive stretch or recoil.

cards.q: What is happening to the muscle during a concentric contraction?
cards.a: It shortens while generating force.
options: It lengthens while generating force
It holds a fixed length while generating force
It shortens without generating force
It shortens while generating force
cards.explanation: Concentric contraction is the familiar case in which crossbridge force exceeds the load, so the muscle shortens and does positive work on the load. Lengthening under load is eccentric. Holding a fixed length is isometric. Shortening with no force generation is elastic recoil, not contraction.

cards.q: What is happening to the muscle during an eccentric contraction?
cards.a: It lengthens while still generating force.
options: It shortens while still generating force
It holds a fixed length while generating force
It lengthens while still generating force
It lengthens after all crossbridges have detached
cards.explanation: In an eccentric contraction the external load exceeds the force the muscle can produce, so the muscle is pulled longer even though crossbridges are attached and resisting, which is how you lower a heavy object under control. Shortening under load is concentric. Holding length is isometric. If every crossbridge detached the muscle would be relaxed, and the lengthening would be uncontrolled.

cards.q: In the load velocity relationship for skeletal muscle, what happens to shortening velocity as the load on the muscle increases?
cards.a: Shortening velocity decreases.
options: Shortening velocity decreases
Shortening velocity increases
Shortening velocity is unchanged until the load exceeds maximal tension
Shortening velocity increases and then plateaus
cards.explanation: Heavier loads mean each crossbridge spends more of its cycle bearing force, so the filaments slide more slowly and the load velocity curve falls steadily from left to right. Velocity cannot rise with load, since more work must be done per unit distance. It also does not stay flat, because even a small load slows shortening measurably. A plateau would imply that load stops mattering, which the curve does not show.

cards.q: At what load does a muscle reach its maximum shortening velocity, usually written Vmax?
cards.a: At zero load.
options: At the load that produces maximum power
At zero load
At the load equal to maximal isometric tension
At the load that is just above maximal isometric tension
cards.explanation: With nothing to lift, crossbridges cycle as fast as their myosin ATPase allows, so Vmax is measured at zero external load. Maximum power occurs near a third of maximal load, where force and velocity are both moderate. At a load equal to maximal isometric tension the muscle cannot shorten at all, so velocity is zero. Above that load the muscle is stretched, which is eccentric rather than shortening.

cards.q: What does the term isotonic contraction describe?
cards.a: A contraction in which the muscle changes length against a constant load.
options: A contraction in which the muscle length is held constant
A contraction in which the muscle changes length against a constant load
A contraction in which tension rises continuously to a peak
A contraction in which the muscle is stimulated at a constant frequency
cards.explanation: Isotonic means same tension: once tension matches the load, the muscle changes length while the force it exerts stays fixed at the load value. Constant length is isometric, the opposite condition. Continuously rising tension describes the early, isometric phase before movement begins. Constant stimulus frequency is a property of the stimulator, not of the mechanics of the contraction.

cards.q: Which type of contraction produces the greatest tension in a maximally activated muscle?
cards.a: Eccentric.
options: Eccentric
Concentric
Isometric
Concentric at very low load
cards.explanation: Eccentric contractions generate the highest tension, roughly 1.2 to 1.8 times maximal isometric force, because stretching an attached crossbridge adds mechanical strain to the force it already produces. Isometric force is the next highest and is the usual reference point. Concentric force is lower than isometric at every velocity, because attached crossbridges are detaching to allow sliding. Concentric contraction at very low load produces the least force of all, since the load itself sets the tension.

cards.q: In an isotonic twitch against a load, what is happening during the delay between the stimulus and the start of shortening?
cards.a: The muscle is contracting isometrically until its tension matches the load.
options: The action potential is still traveling along the motor nerve
Ca2+ is being pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The muscle is contracting isometrically until its tension matches the load
The tendon is being stretched by the falling load
cards.explanation: Nothing can move until muscle tension equals the load, so every isotonic contraction begins with an isometric phase, and the heavier the load, the longer that phase lasts. Nerve conduction is over in a few milliseconds and does not account for the load dependence of the delay. Ca2+ reuptake happens during relaxation, at the end of the twitch. The load is held stationary by a support before the contraction, so it is not stretching the tendon.

cards.q: A student holds a heavy textbook motionless in an outstretched hand. How would you classify the activity of the elbow flexors?
cards.a: Isometric, because tension is high and muscle length is constant.
options: Concentric, because the flexors are actively shortening to hold the book
Isometric, because tension is high and muscle length is constant
Eccentric, because gravity is pulling the forearm down
Isotonic, because the load on the muscle stays constant
cards.explanation: The book is not moving, so the elbow angle and therefore the muscle length are fixed while the flexors generate force, which is the definition of isometric. Concentric requires visible shortening, which is not happening. Gravity pulls downward but the arm is not descending, so no lengthening occurs and it is not eccentric. The load is indeed constant, but isotonic requires a length change, which this contraction does not have.

cards.q: A lifter slowly lowers a dumbbell from a fully flexed elbow to a straight arm, keeping control the whole way. How would you classify the biceps activity?
cards.a: Eccentric, because the biceps lengthens while producing force.
options: Eccentric, because the biceps lengthens while producing force
Concentric, because the biceps is actively producing force
Isometric, because the biceps controls the speed of descent
Passive lengthening, because the biceps is relaxed during lowering
cards.explanation: The elbow is extending, so the biceps is getting longer, and it is still generating force to keep the descent slow, which makes this eccentric. Producing force alone does not make a contraction concentric; the direction of length change decides that. Controlling speed does not make it isometric, since the length is clearly changing. If the biceps were relaxed the dumbbell would drop, so passive lengthening is ruled out by the controlled descent.

cards.q: A person rises from a chair to a standing position. How would you classify the quadriceps activity during the rise?
cards.a: Concentric, because the quadriceps shortens as the knee extends.
options: Eccentric, because the quadriceps resists gravity throughout
Isometric, because the knee is loaded through the whole movement
Concentric, because the quadriceps shortens as the knee extends
Eccentric, because body weight exceeds the force the quadriceps can produce
cards.explanation: Standing up extends the knee, which shortens the quadriceps while it lifts body weight, so this is a concentric contraction doing positive work. Resisting gravity does not by itself make a contraction eccentric; sitting back down would be the eccentric half of the same movement. The knee angle changes markedly, so nothing about this is isometric. If body weight exceeded quadriceps force the person would not rise at all.

cards.q: A muscle shortening against a 2 kg load is then asked to shorten against a 6 kg load. Predict what happens to its shortening velocity and to the tension it develops.
cards.a: Velocity falls and tension rises.
options: Velocity rises and tension falls
Velocity falls and tension also falls
Velocity is unchanged and tension rises
Velocity falls and tension rises
cards.explanation: In an isotonic contraction the tension the muscle develops equals the load it moves, so a heavier load means higher tension, and the load velocity curve says the higher the tension, the slower the shortening. Velocity cannot rise with load, since more force per crossbridge means slower cycling. Tension cannot fall while the load rises, because the muscle must at least match the load to move it. And velocity is strongly load dependent, so it does not stay fixed.

cards.q: A muscle is stimulated maximally while attached to a load heavier than its maximal isometric tension. Predict what the muscle does.
cards.a: It develops tension without shortening, so the contraction remains isometric.
options: It shortens very slowly against the load
It lengthens rapidly because the crossbridges cannot attach
It develops tension without shortening, so the contraction remains isometric
It shortens at Vmax because maximal stimulation overrides the load
cards.explanation: Shortening requires muscle tension to exceed the load, and here it cannot, so tension rises to its maximum and the length never changes, which is an isometric contraction by definition. Slow shortening happens only for loads below maximal isometric tension. The crossbridges do attach, which is exactly why the muscle can hold the load rather than being pulled out rapidly. Vmax is the zero load velocity and is the opposite extreme from this situation.

cards.q: Which type of contraction is most strongly associated with delayed onset muscle soreness one or two days after unfamiliar exercise?
cards.a: Eccentric contractions.
options: Concentric contractions
Isometric contractions held at short muscle length
Low load concentric contractions at high velocity
Eccentric contractions
cards.explanation: Eccentric work loads a small number of attached crossbridges with high force per bridge, which produces microscopic damage to the sarcomeres and the inflammatory response felt a day or two later. Concentric contractions distribute lower force across the working bridges and cause much less damage. Isometric holds at short lengths produce lower tension still, and short lengths are the least damaging. Fast, light concentric work generates the lowest tension of any of these options.

cards.q: A hiker walks steadily downhill. What is the quadriceps doing at each step as the leading knee bends under body weight?
cards.a: Contracting eccentrically to control knee flexion.
options: Contracting concentrically to drive the knee forward
Contracting eccentrically to control knee flexion
Contracting isometrically to lock the knee in place
Relaxing completely while the ligaments absorb the load
cards.explanation: Body weight bends the loaded knee, which lengthens the quadriceps while it keeps generating force to slow the descent, the textbook eccentric contraction and the reason downhill walking causes soreness. Concentric quadriceps work extends the knee, which is what happens going uphill. The knee is flexing rather than holding a fixed angle, so it is not isometric. If the quadriceps relaxed the knee would buckle.

cards.q: A muscle with a maximal isometric tension of 60 N is tested at three loads. At 10 N it shortens at 40 mm/s, at 30 N at 18 mm/s, and at 50 N at 4 mm/s. At which of these loads does the muscle generate the most mechanical power?
cards.a: 30 N, because the product of force and velocity is highest there.
options: 10 N, because shortening velocity is highest there
50 N, because force is highest there
30 N, because the product of force and velocity is highest there
All three are equal, because power depends only on maximal isometric tension
cards.explanation: Power is force times velocity, so the products are 400, 540, and 200 in these units, and the intermediate load wins because it trades a moderate amount of force for a moderate amount of speed. The lightest load gives high velocity but almost no force, and the heaviest gives high force but almost no movement, so both produce less power. Maximal isometric tension is measured at zero velocity, where power is zero by definition.

cards.q: In an isotonic twitch experiment, the load is increased from 5 g to 20 g. Predict how the tracing changes in two respects: the delay before shortening begins and the distance the muscle shortens.
cards.a: The delay lengthens and the shortening distance decreases.
options: The delay shortens and the shortening distance decreases
The delay lengthens and the shortening distance decreases
The delay lengthens and the shortening distance increases
The delay is unchanged and the shortening distance decreases
cards.explanation: A heavier load takes longer for the isometric phase to build tension up to the load value, so the delay grows, and less of the twitch remains for shortening, so the muscle lifts the load a shorter distance before relaxation begins. The delay cannot shorten with a heavier load, since more tension must be developed first. Shortening distance falls rather than rises, because both force and available time are working against the muscle. And the delay is load dependent, so it does not stay fixed.

cards.q: A lifter cannot curl a 30 kg dumbbell but can lower the same dumbbell slowly and under full control. Which sequence of statements explains this?
cards.a: Eccentric force exceeds isometric force, which exceeds concentric force at any shortening velocity.
options: Eccentric force exceeds isometric force, which exceeds concentric force at any shortening velocity
Concentric force exceeds isometric force, which exceeds eccentric force
Isometric force exceeds both eccentric and concentric force
Eccentric and concentric force are equal, and the difference is entirely motor unit recruitment
cards.explanation: Stretching attached crossbridges adds strain to the force they already generate, so a maximally activated muscle can resist more load while lengthening than it can lift while shortening, which is why the lowering succeeds when the lift fails. Concentric force is the smallest of the three, so ranking it highest reverses the relationship. Isometric force sits between the other two rather than above both. Recruitment is maximal in both attempts here, so the difference comes from crossbridge mechanics rather than from how many motor units are active.

cards.q: A muscle is stimulated maximally while an experimenter slowly pulls it longer against the contraction, then repeats the test while allowing it to shorten at 20 mm/s. Compared with a maximal isometric contraction of the same muscle, what tensions would you predict?
cards.a: Higher than isometric during the pull and lower than isometric during the shortening.
options: Lower than isometric during the pull and higher than isometric during the shortening
Higher than isometric in both tests, because the muscle is maximally stimulated
Higher than isometric during the pull and lower than isometric during the shortening
Equal to isometric in both tests, because stimulation rather than velocity sets tension
cards.explanation: Forced lengthening is eccentric and raises tension above the isometric value by straining attached crossbridges, while shortening is concentric and drops tension below isometric because bridges must detach to permit sliding. The reversed answer swaps the two limbs of the force velocity curve. Maximal stimulation sets how many fibers are active but does not exempt the muscle from the velocity dependence of force. That same dependence is why tension is not simply equal in all three conditions.

cards.q: Which skeletal muscle fiber type contains the highest density of mitochondria?
cards.a: Slow oxidative.
options: Slow oxidative
Fast glycolytic
Fast oxidative glycolytic
All three carry the same mitochondrial density
cards.explanation: Slow oxidative fibers are built for sustained aerobic work, so they are packed with mitochondria to keep oxidative phosphorylation supplying ATP for hours. Fast glycolytic fibers sit at the other extreme, with few mitochondria and a reliance on stored glycogen. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers are intermediate, with a substantial but smaller mitochondrial complement than slow oxidative fibers. The three types differ sharply on this measure, which is one of the main ways they are told apart.

cards.q: High myoglobin content, which gives a muscle its red appearance, is characteristic of which fiber type?
cards.a: Slow oxidative.
options: Fast glycolytic
Fast oxidative glycolytic only
Slow oxidative
Fibers with the largest diameter
cards.explanation: Myoglobin stores oxygen inside the fiber and speeds its diffusion to the mitochondria, so the fibers that depend most on oxygen carry the most, and slow oxidative fibers are the reddest. Fast glycolytic fibers have little myoglobin and appear pale or white. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers do contain myoglobin, but less than slow oxidative fibers, so naming them alone is wrong. Diameter tracks with force capacity, and the largest fibers are actually the palest.

cards.q: Fast glycolytic fibers depend mainly on which source of ATP during activity?
cards.a: Anaerobic glycolysis using stored glycogen.
options: Anaerobic glycolysis using stored glycogen
Oxidative phosphorylation using fatty acids
Oxidative phosphorylation using blood glucose
Creatine phosphate alone for the entire contraction
cards.explanation: Fast glycolytic fibers have few mitochondria and a poor capillary supply, so they break down their large glycogen stores anaerobically to lactate, which supplies ATP quickly but only briefly. Fatty acid oxidation requires abundant mitochondria and oxygen, which describes slow oxidative fibers. Oxidative use of blood glucose has the same requirement and the same problem. Creatine phosphate is used by all fiber types, but it lasts only seconds and cannot carry a contraction on its own.

cards.q: Which fiber type fatigues most rapidly during repeated maximal contractions?
cards.a: Fast glycolytic.
options: Fast glycolytic
Slow oxidative
Fast oxidative glycolytic
All three fatigue at the same rate
cards.explanation: Fast glycolytic fibers burn through glycogen quickly and accumulate the metabolic byproducts of anaerobic work, so their force falls within a minute or less. Slow oxidative fibers resist fatigue for hours because oxidative phosphorylation regenerates ATP as fast as it is used. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers are intermediate, holding force for minutes rather than seconds. Fatigue resistance is one of the main axes on which the three types differ.

cards.q: Differences in myosin ATPase activity between fiber types most directly determine what?
cards.a: How fast the fiber shortens.
options: How fast the fiber shortens
How much force one crossbridge produces
How resistant the fiber is to fatigue
How many capillaries surround the fiber
cards.explanation: Myosin ATPase splits ATP at the crossbridge, and the speed of that step sets the speed of the cycle, which is what makes fast fibers fast and slow fibers slow. Force per crossbridge is nearly the same in all fiber types; whole fiber force differences come from fiber diameter and the number of myofibrils. Fatigue resistance is set by metabolic machinery, not by the ATPase rate. Capillary supply is a property of the surrounding tissue, established by the fiber's oxidative demand.

cards.q: Capillary density around the fiber is greatest in which type?
cards.a: Slow oxidative.
options: Fast glycolytic
Slow oxidative
Fast oxidative glycolytic
Whichever type has the largest cross sectional area
cards.explanation: Slow oxidative fibers must be supplied with oxygen and fuel continuously, so they are surrounded by the richest capillary network of the three. Fast glycolytic fibers work anaerobically for short bursts and have the sparsest capillary supply. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers fall between the two. Large diameter actually works against oxygen delivery, because it lengthens the diffusion distance from capillary to the center of the fiber.

cards.q: Which fiber type stores the most glycogen?
cards.a: Fast glycolytic.
options: Fast glycolytic
Slow oxidative
Fast oxidative glycolytic
Fibers with the highest myoglobin content
cards.explanation: Fast glycolytic fibers rely on anaerobic glycolysis, and glycogen is the substrate for that pathway, so they hold the largest intracellular stores. Slow oxidative fibers store less glycogen and lean more on fatty acids and blood borne fuel delivered continuously by their capillaries. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers store an intermediate amount. High myoglobin marks the oxidative end of the spectrum, which is the low glycogen end.

cards.q: Which fiber type has the largest diameter and generates the greatest force per fiber?
cards.a: Fast glycolytic.
options: Slow oxidative
Fast oxidative glycolytic
Fast glycolytic
Fiber diameter is the same in all three types
cards.explanation: Fast glycolytic fibers pack in the most myofibrils, so they are the widest and produce the most force per fiber, which suits them to brief powerful efforts. Slow oxidative fibers are the smallest, a design that keeps oxygen diffusion distances short. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers are intermediate in diameter as in most other properties. Diameter differs substantially among the types and is one reason motor unit force output varies so widely.

cards.q: The soleus muscle works continuously at low force to keep a standing person from falling forward. Which fiber type would you expect to predominate?
cards.a: Slow oxidative.
options: Slow oxidative
Fast glycolytic
Fast oxidative glycolytic
An even mix of fast glycolytic and slow oxidative
cards.explanation: A postural task demands low force sustained for hours, which is exactly what fatigue resistant, oxygen dependent slow oxidative fibers deliver. Fast glycolytic fibers would fatigue within a minute and are wasteful for a low force job. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers hold up better than fast glycolytic but still fatigue faster than the task requires. A mix weighted toward fast fibers would not match the continuous demand.

cards.q: A biopsy from a competitive sprinter's gastrocnemius shows large pale fibers with abundant glycogen and few mitochondria. Which type are they, and what does that predict about fatigue?
cards.a: Fast glycolytic, and they fatigue within about a minute of maximal work.
options: Fast oxidative glycolytic, and they resist fatigue for many minutes
Slow oxidative, and they resist fatigue for hours
Fast glycolytic, and they fatigue within about a minute of maximal work
Fast glycolytic, and they resist fatigue because glycogen stores are large
cards.explanation: Pale color means low myoglobin, few mitochondria means little oxidative capacity, and abundant glycogen means anaerobic fuel, so these are fast glycolytic fibers, which fatigue rapidly. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers would show many more mitochondria and a redder appearance. Slow oxidative fibers would be small, red, and mitochondria rich, the opposite of what is described. Large glycogen stores do not confer fatigue resistance, because the byproducts of anaerobic glycolysis accumulate long before the glycogen runs out.

cards.q: A biopsy shows fibers with a fast myosin ATPase, a high mitochondrial density, and moderate glycogen. Which fiber type is this?
cards.a: Fast oxidative glycolytic.
options: Slow oxidative
Fast glycolytic
A denervated fiber reverting to an immature type
Fast oxidative glycolytic
cards.explanation: Fast ATPase with strong oxidative machinery is the signature of the intermediate type, which contracts quickly yet resists fatigue reasonably well. Slow oxidative fibers would have the oxidative machinery but a slow ATPase. Fast glycolytic fibers would have the fast ATPase but very few mitochondria. Denervated fibers atrophy rather than adopt a distinct hybrid profile, and nothing in the description points to denervation.

cards.q: As a person gradually increases force from a light to a maximal effort, which motor units are recruited first, and why?
cards.a: Slow oxidative units, because their motor neurons reach threshold first.
options: Fast glycolytic units, because they generate the most force per fiber
Fast oxidative glycolytic units, because they balance speed with endurance capacity
Slow oxidative units, because their motor neurons reach threshold first
All units at once, because recruitment follows the all or none law
cards.explanation: The size principle says smaller motor neurons depolarize to threshold at lower synaptic current, and those neurons innervate slow oxidative fibers, so light efforts use the fatigue resistant units first and save the powerful ones for later. Fast glycolytic units do produce the most force, which is precisely why they are held in reserve until high force is needed. Fast oxidative glycolytic units are recruited in the middle of the range, not at the start. The all or none law applies to a single fiber's action potential, not to how many motor units a muscle activates.

cards.q: A fiber is found to have very few mitochondria, sparse capillaries, and a large glycogen store. Predict how long it can sustain maximal force.
cards.a: Under a minute, because anaerobic glycolysis cannot sustain the ATP demand.
options: Under a minute, because anaerobic glycolysis cannot sustain the ATP demand
Several hours, because its glycogen store is large
About ten to fifteen minutes, because it can shift to fatty acid oxidation
Indefinitely, as long as blood glucose remains normal
cards.explanation: Without mitochondria and capillaries the fiber must make ATP anaerobically, and that pathway produces byproducts and drains glycogen fast enough that force falls within seconds to a minute. Glycogen size does not rescue it, because fatigue arrives well before the store is exhausted. Fatty acid oxidation requires mitochondria and oxygen, which this fiber lacks. Blood glucose cannot help much either, since sparse capillaries limit delivery and anaerobic yield per glucose is tiny.

cards.q: A muscle sample looks distinctly pale rather than red. What does that predict about its dominant fiber type and its fatigue resistance?
cards.a: Mostly fast glycolytic fibers, with poor fatigue resistance.
options: Mostly slow oxidative fibers, with excellent fatigue resistance
Mostly fast oxidative glycolytic fibers, with excellent fatigue resistance
Mostly fast glycolytic fibers, with poor fatigue resistance
Mostly fast glycolytic fibers, with excellent fatigue resistance
cards.explanation: Color comes from myoglobin and from the density of capillaries, both of which track oxidative capacity, so a pale muscle is dominated by fast glycolytic fibers that tire quickly. Slow oxidative fibers would make the muscle look dark red. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers also carry myoglobin, so they would not produce a pale sample. Correctly naming the fiber type but pairing it with good fatigue resistance misses the tradeoff that defines the type.

cards.q: Compare the fiber recruitment demanded by a two hour marathon pace and by a single maximal deadlift. Which comparison is correct?
cards.a: The marathon relies chiefly on slow oxidative fibers, while the deadlift recruits fast glycolytic fibers as well.
options: The marathon relies chiefly on fast glycolytic fibers, while the deadlift relies chiefly on slow oxidative fibers
Both rely chiefly on fast oxidative glycolytic fibers, because both require substantial force
The marathon relies chiefly on slow oxidative fibers, while the deadlift recruits fast glycolytic fibers as well
Both recruit all fiber types equally, because recruitment does not depend on the force required
cards.explanation: Long, low force work is exactly the job of fatigue resistant slow oxidative fibers, while a brief maximal lift needs so much force that recruitment proceeds up the size principle to include fast glycolytic units. Reversing the two ignores that fast glycolytic fibers cannot sustain two hours of work. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers contribute to both tasks, but they do not dominate either one. Recruitment is graded by required force, so equal recruitment in both tasks is not what happens.

cards.q: Three fiber samples are measured. Sample X: slow myosin ATPase, very high mitochondrial density, dense capillaries. Sample Y: fast ATPase, high mitochondrial density, moderate capillaries. Sample Z: fast ATPase, low mitochondrial density, sparse capillaries. Which sample would you expect to dominate the calf muscle of a middle distance runner during a hard four minute race?
cards.a: Sample Y, because a four minute effort needs both speed and oxidative capacity.
options: Sample X, because any event lasting several minutes is entirely aerobic in nature
Sample Y, because a four minute effort needs both speed and oxidative capacity
Sample Z, because the effort is described as hard rather than easy
Sample X, because slow fibers are recruited first in every contraction
cards.explanation: Sample Y is fast oxidative glycolytic, and a four minute maximal effort sits exactly in its niche: fast enough to need a rapid ATPase, long enough to need mitochondria. Sample X is slow oxidative and contributes, but its slow ATPase limits the pace of a race effort. Sample Z is fast glycolytic and would fatigue in well under a minute. Slow fibers are indeed recruited first, but by four minutes at race pace the recruitment has moved well past them.

cards.q: A single motor unit is stimulated repeatedly in an isolated muscle. Its twitches are brief, it produces high force, and its force falls by more than half within 45 seconds. Classify the unit and name the metabolic feature that explains the force decline.
cards.a: Fast glycolytic, because its few mitochondria force it to depend on anaerobic glycolysis.
options: Fast oxidative glycolytic, because its intermediate mitochondrial content limits sustained work
Fast glycolytic, because its few mitochondria force it to depend on anaerobic glycolysis
Slow oxidative, because its small fibers exhaust their glycogen quickly
Fast glycolytic, because its myosin ATPase runs out of ATP binding sites
cards.explanation: Brief twitches point to a fast ATPase, high force points to large fibers, and rapid fatigue points to little oxidative capacity, which together define a fast glycolytic unit dependent on anaerobic glycolysis. A fast oxidative glycolytic unit would hold force much longer than 45 seconds. Slow oxidative units produce low force with long twitches and resist fatigue, so they do not match the tracing. Myosin does not run out of binding sites; fatigue arises from metabolic changes inside the fiber, not from a shortage of sites.

cards.q: In a classic cross innervation experiment, the nerve normally supplying a fast muscle is surgically redirected to a slow muscle and allowed to reinnervate it. Over weeks the slow muscle's contraction speed increases and its myosin isoform shifts. What does this result show?
cards.a: The pattern of neural activity the motor neuron delivers can drive a change in fiber type.
options: Fiber type is fixed at birth and the observed change must be an artifact of surgery
Fiber type is determined only by the blood supply reaching the muscle
The pattern of neural activity the motor neuron delivers can drive a change in fiber type
The muscle changed type because its capillary density changed first
cards.explanation: Reinnervation by a nerve with a different firing pattern converts the muscle toward the properties of the donor nerve's usual target, which shows that chronic activity pattern regulates myosin isoform expression and metabolic profile. Fiber type is clearly not fixed, since the change is measurable and reproducible. Blood supply matters for oxidative capacity but was not the variable manipulated here. Capillary density adapts to activity as well, so it is a consequence of the new activity pattern, not the cause of the myosin switch.

cards.q: A subject squeezes a handgrip at 15 percent of maximum for two minutes, then jumps to 90 percent of maximum. Predict what happens to the fiber types in use and to the rate of lactate production.
cards.a: Recruitment extends from slow oxidative to fast glycolytic units, and lactate production rises sharply.
options: Recruitment shifts from fast glycolytic back to slow oxidative units, and lactate production falls
Recruitment stays limited to slow oxidative units, and lactate production is unchanged
Recruitment extends from slow oxidative to fast glycolytic units, and lactate production rises sharply
Recruitment extends to fast glycolytic units, but lactate production falls because more motor units share the work
cards.explanation: Raising force recruits progressively larger motor units, so the fast glycolytic units added at 90 percent bring their anaerobic metabolism with them and blood lactate climbs. Recruitment never runs backward down the size principle when force is increasing. Staying limited to slow oxidative units could not generate 90 percent of maximal force. Adding motor units increases total ATP turnover rather than spreading a fixed demand, so lactate production rises rather than falls.

cards.q: Which ATP source supplies the working muscle fastest at the very start of a contraction?
cards.a: Creatine phosphate.
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Oxidative phosphorylation
Fatty acid oxidation
Creatine phosphate
cards.explanation: Creatine phosphate transfers its phosphate to ADP in a single enzymatic step, so it regenerates ATP faster than any other route, though the store is small. Anaerobic glycolysis is next fastest but takes several reactions to get going. Oxidative phosphorylation is the slowest to respond, since it depends on delivering oxygen and on many mitochondrial steps. Fatty acid oxidation is the slowest of all, because the fatty acids must first be mobilized and transported into mitochondria.

cards.q: Which enzyme transfers a phosphate group from creatine phosphate to ADP in a working muscle fiber?
cards.a: Creatine kinase.
options: Myosin ATPase
Phosphofructokinase
Creatine kinase
ATP synthase
cards.explanation: Creatine kinase catalyzes the reversible transfer that rebuilds ATP from ADP and creatine phosphate, which is why it is the enzyme of the first few seconds of effort. Myosin ATPase splits ATP at the crossbridge rather than regenerating it. Phosphofructokinase is the rate limiting enzyme of glycolysis, a different pathway. ATP synthase makes ATP in mitochondria using the proton gradient, not using creatine phosphate.

cards.q: For roughly how long can stored creatine phosphate sustain maximal muscle activity?
cards.a: About 10 to 15 seconds.
options: About 1 to 2 seconds
About 2 to 3 minutes
About 10 to 15 seconds
About 20 to 30 minutes
cards.explanation: Creatine phosphate stores cover the first 10 to 15 seconds of maximal effort, roughly the length of a short sprint, before glycolysis has to take over. One to two seconds is closer to the amount of preformed ATP already sitting in the fiber. Two to three minutes is the range covered by anaerobic glycolysis. Twenty to thirty minutes and beyond belongs to oxidative phosphorylation.

cards.q: What is the end product of anaerobic glycolysis in a working muscle fiber?
cards.a: Lactate.
options: Pyruvate entering the mitochondrion
Carbon dioxide and water
Lactate
Acetyl CoA
cards.explanation: When oxygen supply lags behind demand, pyruvate is reduced to lactate so that NAD+ is regenerated and glycolysis can keep running. Pyruvate entering the mitochondrion is what happens when oxygen is adequate, which makes the pathway aerobic rather than anaerobic. Carbon dioxide and water are the end products of complete oxidation. Acetyl CoA is formed from pyruvate inside the mitochondrion, again an aerobic step.

cards.q: What is the net ATP yield per glucose molecule from anaerobic glycolysis?
cards.a: 2 ATP.
options: 2 ATP
4 ATP
18 ATP
30 to 32 ATP
cards.explanation: Glycolysis generates four ATP but spends two in its early steps, so the net yield is two ATP per glucose when the pathway ends at lactate. Four is the gross figure before the investment is subtracted. Eighteen does not correspond to any standard figure in this pathway. Thirty to thirty two is the yield when glucose is fully oxidized aerobically.

cards.q: Approximately how much ATP does complete oxidative metabolism of one glucose molecule yield?
cards.a: About 30 to 32 ATP.
options: About 2 ATP
About 12 ATP
About 100 ATP
About 30 to 32 ATP
cards.explanation: Full oxidation through glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and the electron transport chain yields roughly 30 to 32 ATP per glucose, about fifteen times the anaerobic yield. Two ATP is the anaerobic figure. Twelve does not match either pathway. About 100 ATP per glucose overstates the yield by a wide margin, although a single long chain fatty acid can approach that range.

cards.q: Which ATP source can sustain muscle activity for hours as long as fuel and oxygen keep arriving?
cards.a: Oxidative phosphorylation.
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Oxidative phosphorylation
Creatine phosphate
The preformed ATP already in the fiber
cards.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation regenerates ATP at a modest rate but can do so indefinitely, which is why endurance work depends on it. Anaerobic glycolysis is limited to a couple of minutes at high intensity by byproduct accumulation and glycogen depletion. Creatine phosphate lasts seconds. Preformed ATP is the smallest store of all and would be exhausted in a second or two without regeneration.

cards.q: Which of these ATP sources requires oxygen delivery to the muscle fiber?
cards.a: Oxidative phosphorylation.
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Transfer of phosphate from creatine phosphate
Hydrolysis of preformed ATP by myosin
Oxidative phosphorylation
cards.explanation: Only oxidative phosphorylation uses oxygen, as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, which is why its rate is limited by blood flow and oxygen delivery. Anaerobic glycolysis is defined by proceeding without oxygen. The creatine kinase reaction is a single phosphate transfer with no oxygen requirement. Myosin splits ATP mechanically and chemically, again with no oxygen involved.

cards.q: An athlete performs an all out 8 second effort from rest. Which ATP source supplies most of the energy?
cards.a: Creatine phosphate.
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Oxidative phosphorylation
Fatty acid oxidation
Creatine phosphate
cards.explanation: Eight seconds falls inside the creatine phosphate window, since that system responds instantly and covers roughly the first 10 to 15 seconds of maximal work. Anaerobic glycolysis is contributing by then but has not yet become the main supplier. Oxidative phosphorylation takes tens of seconds to ramp up and cannot match the ATP demand of an all out sprint. Fatty acid oxidation is slower still and dominates only during prolonged low intensity work.

cards.q: A runner sprints as hard as possible for 60 seconds. Which ATP source dominates over most of that effort, and what accumulates as a result?
cards.a: Anaerobic glycolysis, with lactate accumulating in muscle and blood.
options: Oxidative phosphorylation, with carbon dioxide accumulating in muscle and blood
Anaerobic glycolysis, with lactate accumulating in muscle and blood
Creatine phosphate, with creatine accumulating in the fiber
Fatty acid oxidation, with ketone bodies accumulating in blood
cards.explanation: A 60 second maximal effort outruns both the creatine phosphate store and the rate of oxidative ATP supply, so anaerobic glycolysis carries the bulk of the load and lactate builds up. Oxidative phosphorylation contributes but cannot meet the demand at that intensity. Creatine phosphate is largely spent within the first 15 seconds. Fatty acid oxidation is far too slow to matter in a maximal effort of this length.

cards.q: A person jogs at a comfortable pace for 30 minutes. Which ATP source supplies most of the energy?
cards.a: Oxidative phosphorylation.
options: Anaerobic glycolysis
Creatine phosphate
Anaerobic glycolysis for the first half and creatine phosphate for the second
Oxidative phosphorylation
cards.explanation: At a submaximal pace, oxygen delivery keeps up with demand, so mitochondria supply nearly all the ATP and the effort can continue for a long time. Anaerobic glycolysis would flood the muscle with lactate long before 30 minutes elapsed. Creatine phosphate lasts seconds and only covers the first few strides. The final option reverses the physiology entirely, since creatine phosphate is a starting system rather than an ending one.

cards.q: Predict what happens to blood lactate during a maximal 400 meter run lasting about 50 seconds.
cards.a: It rises substantially, because anaerobic glycolysis is supplying a large share of the ATP.
options: It falls, because lactate is consumed as fuel during intense exercise
It stays flat, because oxidative phosphorylation covers the whole demand
It rises only after the run ends, because lactate cannot leave muscle during contraction
It rises substantially, because anaerobic glycolysis is supplying a large share of the ATP
cards.explanation: A 50 second maximal effort demands ATP far faster than oxidative phosphorylation can deliver, so glycolysis runs at high rate and lactate accumulates in muscle and spills into blood. Lactate is used as fuel by heart and by other muscle fibers, but at this intensity production far exceeds consumption. Oxidative metabolism cannot cover a maximal effort of this length. Lactate does leave the fiber on monocarboxylate transporters during the run, so the rise is not delayed to the recovery period.

cards.q: An experimental agent blocks creatine kinase in a muscle fiber. Predict the effect on ATP availability during the first five seconds of maximal contraction.
cards.a: ATP falls faster than normal, because the creatine phosphate buffer cannot be tapped.
options: ATP falls faster than normal, because the creatine phosphate buffer cannot be tapped
ATP is unaffected, because glycolysis compensates within milliseconds
ATP rises, because creatine phosphate accumulates unused
ATP falls only after 30 seconds, when glycogen stores are depleted
cards.explanation: Creatine kinase is the only route from creatine phosphate to ATP, so blocking it removes the buffer that normally holds ATP nearly constant through the first seconds of effort. Glycolysis needs several seconds to reach a high rate and cannot fill the gap instantly. Accumulating unused creatine phosphate does not help, because its phosphate can no longer be transferred. Glycogen depletion is a much later event and is not what makes the first five seconds fail.

cards.q: Anaerobic glycolysis yields 2 ATP per glucose and complete oxidation yields about 32. About how many times more glucose per minute must a muscle consume to make the same ATP anaerobically?
cards.a: About 16 times more.
options: About 2 times more
About 16 times more
About 8 times more
About 32 times more
cards.explanation: Dividing 32 by 2 gives 16, so an anaerobic fiber must run through roughly sixteen glucose molecules to match the ATP from one oxidized aerobically, which is why glycogen empties so fast during intense work. Two is the anaerobic yield itself rather than the ratio. Eight would be the ratio if aerobic yield were 16 ATP. Thirty two is the aerobic yield, not the ratio between the pathways.

cards.q: Blood flow to a working muscle is partially occluded so that oxygen delivery falls. Predict the shift in how the fiber makes ATP and the immediate consequence.
cards.a: A shift toward anaerobic glycolysis, with faster glycogen use and lactate accumulation.
options: A shift toward oxidative phosphorylation, with faster fatty acid use
A shift toward creatine phosphate, which can now sustain the contraction indefinitely
A shift toward anaerobic glycolysis, with faster glycogen use and lactate accumulation
No shift, because ATP production rate is set by contraction frequency rather than oxygen supply
cards.explanation: Reduced oxygen limits the electron transport chain, so the fiber leans on the pathway that does not need oxygen, burning glycogen quickly and generating lactate. Oxidative phosphorylation cannot increase when its oxygen supply has been cut. Creatine phosphate does buffer briefly, but the store is small and cannot sustain anything indefinitely. Contraction frequency sets ATP demand, while oxygen availability constrains which pathway can meet it.

cards.q: Two athletes are tested. Athlete A shows blood lactate of 12 mmol/L and a respiratory exchange ratio near 1.0 at the end of the test. Athlete B shows blood lactate of 2 mmol/L and a ratio near 0.85 at the end of a longer test. Which conclusion about the dominant ATP pathway in each is best supported?
cards.a: Athlete A relied heavily on anaerobic glycolysis, while athlete B relied chiefly on oxidative phosphorylation.
options: Athlete A relied chiefly on oxidative phosphorylation, while athlete B relied heavily on anaerobic glycolysis
Both relied chiefly on creatine phosphate, since both completed the tests successfully
Neither conclusion can be drawn, because lactate reflects only liver metabolism
Athlete A relied heavily on anaerobic glycolysis, while athlete B relied chiefly on oxidative phosphorylation
cards.explanation: High lactate with a ratio near 1.0 marks heavy carbohydrate use and a large anaerobic contribution, while low lactate with a ratio near 0.85 indicates a substantial contribution from fat oxidation and an aerobic effort. Reversing the two ignores what a rising lactate concentration signifies. Creatine phosphate could not sustain either test, since both lasted far longer than 15 seconds. Muscle is a major lactate source during exercise, so the measurement does bear on muscle metabolism.

cards.q: A patient with a deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase cannot break down muscle glycogen. During an ischemic forearm exercise test, predict the blood lactate response and the reason.
cards.a: Lactate fails to rise, because glycogen cannot be fed into glycolysis.
options: Lactate rises higher than normal, because oxidative metabolism is also blocked
Lactate fails to rise, because glycogen cannot be fed into glycolysis
Lactate rises normally, because blood glucose substitutes fully for muscle glycogen
Lactate falls below baseline, because the muscle switches entirely to creatine phosphate
cards.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis in working muscle runs mostly on glycogen, so if glycogen cannot be mobilized, the pathway has little substrate and the usual exercise induced lactate rise is absent. Oxidative metabolism is not blocked by this enzyme deficiency, so there is no reason for lactate to overshoot. Blood glucose uptake continues but is far too slow under ischemia to replace glycogen. Creatine phosphate contributes for seconds only and does not lower baseline lactate.

cards.q: At the start of moderate intensity exercise, oxygen uptake takes about two minutes to reach a steady value, yet the muscle produces the required ATP from the first second. Which combination best explains the gap?
cards.a: Creatine phosphate covers the first seconds and glycolysis bridges until oxidative supply reaches steady state.
options: Oxidative phosphorylation is already at steady state and the delay in oxygen uptake is purely a measurement artifact
Fatty acid oxidation covers the first two minutes and is then replaced by carbohydrate oxidation
Stored ATP alone covers the first two minutes, after which oxidative phosphorylation begins
Creatine phosphate covers the first seconds and glycolysis bridges until oxidative supply reaches steady state
cards.explanation: The lag in oxygen uptake creates an oxygen deficit that is filled by the two systems that do not depend on oxygen, so creatine phosphate covers the first seconds and glycolysis carries the load until mitochondrial ATP output catches up. The lag is a real physiological delay in delivery and mitochondrial activation, not an artifact. Fatty acid oxidation is a slow system and cannot cover the onset of exercise. Stored ATP would last a second or two at most, nowhere near two minutes.

cards.q: A muscle needs 5 mmol of ATP per minute during a task. Creatine phosphate stores can supply about 1 mmol total, anaerobic glycolysis can supply up to 8 mmol per minute for about two minutes, and oxidative phosphorylation can supply 4 mmol per minute indefinitely. Predict what limits performance if the task must continue for 10 minutes.
cards.a: Performance fails after a few minutes, because oxidative supply alone falls short of the 5 mmol per minute demand.
options: Performance fails after a few minutes, because oxidative supply alone falls short of the 5 mmol per minute demand
Performance continues indefinitely, because oxidative phosphorylation alone can meet the demand
Performance fails within 15 seconds, because creatine phosphate is the only usable source for this task
Performance continues indefinitely, because anaerobic glycolysis can be sustained for the full 10 minutes
cards.explanation: Oxidative supply of 4 mmol per minute leaves a 1 mmol per minute shortfall that glycolysis must cover, and glycolysis can only do so for about two minutes, after which the deficit forces the effort to slow or stop. Oxidative supply alone is not enough, since 4 is less than 5. Creatine phosphate is only 1 mmol total and is not the only source available. Glycolysis is explicitly limited to about two minutes at high rate, so it cannot cover the full task.

cards.q: What defines central fatigue?
cards.a: A decline in force caused by reduced drive from the central nervous system to the motor neurons.
options: A decline in force caused by reduced drive from the central nervous system to the motor neurons
A decline in force caused by depletion of ATP within the muscle fiber
A decline in force caused by failure of transmission at the neuromuscular junction
A decline in force caused by accumulation of inorganic phosphate in the sarcoplasm
cards.explanation: Central fatigue lives above the motor neuron: the brain sends fewer or slower commands, so fewer motor units fire even though the muscle itself could still produce force. ATP depletion and phosphate accumulation are events inside the fiber and belong to peripheral fatigue. Neuromuscular junction failure is also peripheral, since it occurs downstream of the central nervous system.

cards.q: Peripheral fatigue is located where in the pathway from brain to force?
cards.a: At or beyond the neuromuscular junction, within the muscle fiber itself.
options: In the motor cortex and descending motor pathways
At or beyond the neuromuscular junction, within the muscle fiber itself
In the sensory pathways carrying pain signals to the brain
In the cardiovascular centers of the medulla
cards.explanation: Peripheral fatigue covers everything from the neuromuscular junction outward, including excitation contraction coupling and the crossbridge machinery inside the fiber. Motor cortex and descending pathways are the site of central fatigue. Sensory pain pathways can contribute to the central component but are not the peripheral site. Medullary cardiovascular centers control blood pressure and heart rate rather than force production.

cards.q: What does excess post exercise oxygen consumption describe?
cards.a: Oxygen consumption that stays above resting level after exercise has ended.
options: Oxygen consumption that stays above resting level after exercise has ended
The oxygen deficit that builds during the first minutes of exercise
The maximal rate of oxygen consumption a person can achieve
The difference between arterial and venous oxygen content during exercise
cards.explanation: After exercise stops, oxygen uptake falls only gradually, and that elevated consumption is used to restore the systems that ran ahead of oxygen delivery during the effort. The oxygen deficit is the mirror image and occurs at the start of exercise. Maximal oxygen consumption is a capacity measure, not a recovery phenomenon. The arteriovenous oxygen difference describes extraction by tissue rather than what happens after exercise.

cards.q: Accumulation of which ion in the T tubule lumen contributes to peripheral fatigue by reducing the size of the action potential?
options: Ca2+
K+
Cl-
HCO3-
cards.explanation: Repeated action potentials pump K+ out of the fiber into the narrow T tubule lumen, where it accumulates, depolarizes the membrane, and inactivates Na+ channels so later action potentials are smaller. Ca2+ accumulates in the sarcoplasm rather than in the T tubule and its problem is impaired release, not impaired excitation. Cl- movement stabilizes the membrane rather than accumulating to a fatiguing level. HCO3- is a buffer and plays no role in T tubule excitation.

cards.q: Accumulating inorganic phosphate inside a fatiguing muscle fiber reduces force mainly by what mechanism?
cards.a: It lowers Ca2+ release and reduces crossbridge force.
options: It lowers Ca2+ release and reduces crossbridge force
It blocks the myosin binding site on actin directly
It prevents the action potential from spreading into the T tubules
It prevents ATP from binding to the myosin head
cards.explanation: Inorganic phosphate rises as ATP and creatine phosphate are broken down, and it both precipitates with Ca2+ inside the sarcoplasmic reticulum and shifts crossbridge kinetics toward lower force. It does not sit on the actin binding site; that is the job of tropomyosin under resting conditions. Action potential conduction into the T tubules is affected by K+ rather than by phosphate. ATP still binds myosin during fatigue, which is why the muscle relaxes rather than going into rigor.

cards.q: During intense exercise, what happens to intracellular pH in a working muscle fiber?
cards.a: It falls, because H+ accumulates alongside high rates of glycolysis.
options: It rises, because lactate consumes H+ as it forms
It stays constant, because muscle has no significant buffering capacity
It rises, because carbon dioxide is exhaled faster during exercise
It falls, because H+ accumulates alongside high rates of glycolysis
cards.explanation: High rates of ATP turnover and glycolysis release H+ faster than the fiber can buffer or export it, so intracellular pH drops during intense work. Lactate formation actually consumes some H+, but the net effect of the whole pathway during intense exercise is acidification. Muscle does have substantial buffering, which slows but does not prevent the fall. Increased ventilation removes carbon dioxide from blood but cannot keep pace with intramuscular H+ production during maximal work.

cards.q: Which of these processes consumes oxygen during the recovery period after exercise?
cards.a: Rebuilding creatine phosphate stores in muscle.
options: Anaerobic conversion of pyruvate to lactate
Rebuilding creatine phosphate stores in muscle
Transfer of phosphate from creatine phosphate to ADP
Diffusion of oxygen from alveolus to capillary
cards.explanation: Restoring creatine phosphate requires ATP made oxidatively, which is a major reason oxygen uptake stays elevated after exercise ends. Converting pyruvate to lactate is by definition an anaerobic step and consumes no oxygen. The creatine kinase reaction that spends creatine phosphate uses no oxygen either; it is the rebuilding that costs. Diffusion across the alveolar membrane is a transport step, not a process that consumes oxygen.

cards.q: Which experimental maneuver is used to separate central from peripheral fatigue in a voluntarily contracting muscle?
cards.a: Delivering an electrical stimulus to the motor nerve during a maximal voluntary effort.
options: Measuring blood lactate immediately after the effort
Delivering an electrical stimulus to the motor nerve during a maximal voluntary effort
Recording the resting membrane potential of a single fiber
Measuring the muscle's cross sectional area before and after the effort
cards.explanation: A stimulus superimposed on a maximal voluntary contraction adds force only if the nervous system was failing to activate every motor unit, so any extra force is a direct measure of the central component. Blood lactate reports metabolic activity but says nothing about how completely the nervous system is driving the muscle. Resting membrane potential of one fiber does not distinguish the two sites either. Cross sectional area changes over weeks of training, not over a single fatiguing contraction.

cards.q: A subject's maximal voluntary grip force has fallen by 30 percent after a sustained effort. An electrical stimulus applied to the nerve adds a large extra increment of force. What does this indicate?
cards.a: A substantial central component, because the nervous system is no longer fully activating the muscle.
options: A purely peripheral component, because the muscle can still respond to stimulation
A substantial central component, because the nervous system is no longer fully activating the muscle
Complete neuromuscular junction failure, because extra force required artificial stimulation
A measurement error, because stimulation cannot add force to a maximal contraction
cards.explanation: If the muscle can produce more force when stimulated than the subject can produce voluntarily, the missing force was never commanded, which is the definition of central fatigue. The muscle responding to stimulation is exactly what rules out a purely peripheral explanation. Junction failure would prevent the stimulus from producing extra force at all. Stimulation adding force to a supposedly maximal effort is the expected finding in central fatigue, not an artifact.

cards.q: After a sustained contraction, voluntary force has fallen by 40 percent and an electrical stimulus to the nerve adds essentially no extra force. Where does the fatigue lie?
cards.a: Peripherally, within the muscle fiber and its excitation contraction coupling.
options: Peripherally, within the muscle fiber and its excitation contraction coupling
Centrally, in descending drive from the motor cortex
Centrally, in the motivation of the subject
In the sensory nerves reporting muscle tension to the brain
cards.explanation: When maximal stimulation cannot recover the lost force, the deficit must lie in the muscle itself, so the fatigue is peripheral. Reduced central drive would leave force in reserve that stimulation could recruit, which is not what happened. Motivation is a central explanation and fails for the same reason. Sensory feedback can influence central drive, but the test result already shows the muscle cannot produce more force even when maximally driven.

cards.q: Inorganic phosphate concentration inside a fatiguing fiber rises sharply. Predict the effect on Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and on peak tension.
cards.a: Ca2+ release falls and peak tension falls.
options: Ca2+ release falls and peak tension falls
Ca2+ release rises and peak tension rises
Ca2+ release falls but peak tension is preserved by increased Ca2+ sensitivity
Ca2+ release is unchanged and peak tension falls only because ATP is depleted
cards.explanation: Phosphate entering the sarcoplasmic reticulum precipitates with Ca2+ there, so less Ca2+ is available for release, and less Ca2+ in the sarcoplasm means fewer active crossbridges and lower tension. Neither release nor tension increases with phosphate. Ca2+ sensitivity actually falls during fatigue rather than rising to compensate. ATP concentration is defended fairly well during fatigue, so it is not the main cause of the tension loss.

cards.q: A sprinter finishes a 200 meter race and then stands still, breathing hard for several minutes. Why does oxygen consumption remain elevated?
cards.a: Oxygen is being used to rebuild creatine phosphate, reload myoglobin and hemoglobin, and clear lactate.
options: Oxygen is being stored in muscle for the next race
Oxygen is being used to rebuild creatine phosphate, reload myoglobin and hemoglobin, and clear lactate
Oxygen consumption tracks heart rate, which is slow to fall for purely mechanical reasons
Oxygen is being consumed by anaerobic glycolysis continuing in the leg muscles
cards.explanation: Recovery costs are real work: creatine phosphate must be resynthesized, oxygen stores on myoglobin and hemoglobin must be refilled, lactate must be converted back to pyruvate or glucose, and elevated body temperature and catecholamines keep metabolic rate high. Oxygen cannot be stockpiled beyond the small myoglobin and hemoglobin stores. Heart rate stays elevated because metabolic demand is elevated, not the other way round.
