Anaerobic glycolysis by definition does not consume oxygen.

cards.q: During a sustained maximal contraction, which fiber type would you predict to lose force first?
cards.a: Fast glycolytic, because it depends on anaerobic metabolism.
options: Slow oxidative, because it is recruited first and therefore works longest
Fast oxidative glycolytic, because it has the highest ATP demand of the three
Fast glycolytic, because it depends on anaerobic metabolism
All types together, because fatigue is a whole muscle rather than a fiber level event
cards.explanation: Fast glycolytic fibers have the least oxidative capacity and the fastest byproduct accumulation, so their force falls within seconds to a minute of maximal work. Slow oxidative fibers are recruited first but are the most fatigue resistant, so they hold force longest. Fast oxidative glycolytic fibers fall between the two rather than leading. Fatigue develops at the level of individual fibers and differs measurably between them, which is why whole muscle force decays in stages.

cards.q: During a sustained submaximal effort a subject's force is falling. A researcher shouts encouragement and force immediately rises. What does that tell you about the fatigue present?
cards.a: At least part of it is central, since increased drive recovered force instantly.
options: At least part of it is central, since increased drive recovered force instantly
It is entirely peripheral, since the muscle was able to produce more force
It reflects rapid resynthesis of creatine phosphate during the shout
It shows that lactate was cleared from the fiber within seconds
cards.explanation: Force that can be recovered by motivation alone was being withheld by the nervous system, so the deficit was central rather than a failure of the muscle. If the fatigue were entirely peripheral, no amount of encouragement could raise force. Creatine phosphate resynthesis takes minutes and requires oxygen, not seconds of shouting. Lactate clearance is likewise far too slow to explain an instant change in force.

cards.q: A subject produces 300 N in a maximal voluntary contraction when rested, and a superimposed nerve stimulus adds 0 N. After two minutes of sustained effort, voluntary force is 180 N and the superimposed stimulus adds 40 N. How much of the 120 N loss is central and how much is peripheral?
cards.a: 40 N central and 80 N peripheral.
options: 120 N central and 0 N peripheral
40 N central and 80 N peripheral
0 N central and 120 N peripheral
80 N central and 40 N peripheral
cards.explanation: The stimulus reveals 40 N the nervous system failed to command, so that is the central share, and the muscle's own maximal capacity has fallen from 300 N to 220 N, an 80 N peripheral loss. Calling the whole 120 N central would require the stimulated muscle to still reach 300 N, which it does not. Calling it all peripheral ignores the 40 N that stimulation recovered. Reversing the two numbers misreads which value the superimposed twitch measures.

cards.q: A sprinter's oxygen consumption after a 100 meter race falls steeply for the first two minutes and then declines slowly over the next 30 minutes. Which explanation best fits the two phases?
cards.a: The fast phase refills creatine phosphate and oxygen stores, and the slow phase reflects lactate handling and raised temperature.
options: The fast phase reflects clearance of lactate from the blood, while the slow phase refills the creatine phosphate stores
The fast phase refills creatine phosphate and oxygen stores, and the slow phase reflects lactate handling and raised temperature
Both phases reflect continued anaerobic glycolysis in the leg muscles
The fast phase reflects the oxygen deficit incurred at the start of the race, while the slow phase is a measurement drift
cards.explanation: Creatine phosphate resynthesis and the reloading of myoglobin and hemoglobin are quick, so they dominate the steep early fall, while lactate conversion, elevated body temperature, and lingering hormonal effects keep metabolic rate slightly high for much longer. Swapping the phases misjudges the timescales, since creatine phosphate recovers in minutes, not half an hour. Anaerobic glycolysis consumes no oxygen, so it cannot account for either phase. The oxygen deficit describes the beginning of exercise and is repaid across both phases rather than only the first.

cards.q: A patient reports profound exercise fatigue. During testing, maximal voluntary force is low, but supramaximal stimulation of the motor nerve produces normal force, and the force decays no faster than normal with repeated stimulation. Where does the problem lie?
cards.a: Above the motor neuron, since the muscle performs normally when driven artificially.
options: At the neuromuscular junction, since voluntary force is reduced
In excitation contraction coupling, since the patient reports fatigue with exertion
In the mitochondria of the muscle fibers, since exercise tolerance is poor
Above the motor neuron, since the muscle performs normally when driven artificially
cards.explanation: Normal stimulated force and a normal rate of decline show that the nerve terminal, the fiber membrane, the coupling machinery, and the crossbridges are all working, so the deficit must be in the drive reaching the motor neurons. A junction problem would show reduced or rapidly declining stimulated force. A coupling defect would depress stimulated force from the first stimulus. A mitochondrial defect would make stimulated force fall abnormally fast during repeated stimulation, which the test excludes.

cards.q: A blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic pressure on the upper arm while the subject performs repeated handgrip contractions. Compared with the same test without the cuff, predict the rate of force loss and the mechanism.
cards.a: Force falls faster, because oxygen delivery is cut and the fiber must rely on anaerobic metabolism.
options: Force falls faster, because the cuff blocks motor nerve conduction within seconds
Force falls more slowly, because trapped blood keeps oxygen available to the muscle
Force falls at the same rate, because muscle fatigue is determined centrally
Force falls faster, because oxygen delivery is cut and the fiber must rely on anaerobic metabolism
cards.explanation: Occluding arterial inflow starves the mitochondria, forces a shift to anaerobic glycolysis, and lets H+, phosphate, and K+ accumulate without washout, so peripheral fatigue develops much faster than usual. Nerve conduction does eventually fail under prolonged compression, but that takes many minutes, far longer than the force decline in this test. Trapped blood is quickly stripped of its oxygen and cannot sustain the muscle. Fatigue in this setting is dominated by the peripheral consequences of ischemia rather than by central drive.

cards.q: What is the principal change in a muscle fiber produced by months of heavy resistance training?
cards.a: An increase in fiber diameter from added myofibrils.
options: An increase in fiber diameter from added myofibrils
An increase in the number of fibers from cell division
An increase in mitochondrial density within each fiber
An increase in the number of sarcomeres in series along the fiber
cards.explanation: Resistance training drives synthesis of new actin and myosin, which are assembled into additional myofibrils, so the fiber grows thicker and produces more force. Mature skeletal muscle fibers do not divide, so the fiber count changes very little. Mitochondrial density is the hallmark of endurance training and often falls slightly with hypertrophy because the fiber grows around the existing mitochondria. Adding sarcomeres in series lengthens a fiber and follows chronic stretch rather than heavy loading.

cards.q: What are the two most characteristic adaptations to months of endurance training within the trained muscle?
cards.a: More mitochondria and a denser capillary network.
options: Larger fiber diameter and greater glycogen storage
More motor units and larger motor neurons
More mitochondria and a denser capillary network
More sarcomeres in series and a longer resting length
cards.explanation: Endurance training improves the muscle's ability to make ATP aerobically, so mitochondrial content and capillary supply both rise, which raises oxygen delivery and oxidative enzyme capacity together. Fiber diameter changes little with endurance work and is the resistance training adaptation. Motor unit number is fixed by the number of motor neurons and does not increase with training. Sarcomere number in series changes with chronic length rather than with endurance activity.

cards.q: What is the difference between hypertrophy and hyperplasia in skeletal muscle?
cards.a: Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of existing fibers, and hyperplasia is an increase in fiber number.
options: Hypertrophy is an increase in fiber number, and hyperplasia is an increase in fiber size
Hypertrophy is an increase in the size of existing fibers, and hyperplasia is an increase in fiber number
Hypertrophy is growth in length, and hyperplasia is growth in diameter
Hypertrophy occurs only with endurance training, and hyperplasia only with resistance training
cards.explanation: Hypertrophy means bigger cells, and it is the dominant response of human skeletal muscle to resistance training, while hyperplasia means more cells and contributes little in humans. Reversing the definitions inverts both terms. Neither term specifies length versus diameter; both describe how mass is added. Hypertrophy is chiefly a resistance training response rather than an endurance one, and hyperplasia is not the endurance response either.

cards.q: What is the main structural change in a muscle immobilized in a cast for several weeks?
cards.a: Fiber diameter decreases as protein breakdown exceeds synthesis.
options: Fiber diameter decreases as protein breakdown exceeds synthesis
Fiber number decreases as unused fibers are removed
Fiber diameter increases as connective tissue is deposited inside the fiber
Mitochondrial density increases to compensate for the reduced workload
cards.explanation: Disuse tips the balance toward protein degradation, so myofibrillar protein is lost and the fibers become thinner, which is why a limb looks smaller when the cast comes off. Fibers atrophy rather than disappear, so the count is roughly preserved. Connective tissue does increase around the muscle with prolonged disuse, but that occurs outside the fibers and does not make them wider. Mitochondrial density falls with disuse rather than rising, because the demand that maintains it is gone.

cards.q: What happens to fiber diameter with several months of pure endurance training?
cards.a: It changes little and may decrease slightly.
options: It increases markedly, similar to resistance training
It changes little and may decrease slightly
It doubles, because oxidative fibers grow fastest
It increases in fast fibers only and is unchanged in slow fibers
cards.explanation: Endurance training improves the aerobic machinery rather than the contractile mass, and a slightly smaller fiber actually shortens the oxygen diffusion path, so diameter stays flat or drops a little. Marked growth in diameter is the resistance training signature. Doubling of diameter does not happen with any training program in that timeframe. Endurance work does not selectively enlarge fast fibers; if anything it shifts them toward a more oxidative profile.

cards.q: What role do satellite cells play in skeletal muscle adaptation?
cards.a: They are muscle stem cells that fuse with fibers and add nuclei.
options: They are immune cells that clear damaged proteins from the fiber
They are the cells that form new capillaries around the fiber
They are sensory receptors that report muscle length back to the spinal cord
They are muscle stem cells that fuse with fibers and add nuclei
cards.explanation: Satellite cells sit under the basal lamina of the fiber, and when the fiber is loaded or injured they proliferate and fuse into it, supplying the extra nuclei that a larger fiber needs to sustain protein synthesis. Clearing damaged protein is the job of macrophages and the fiber's own proteasomes. New capillaries are formed by endothelial cells. Muscle length is reported by muscle spindles, which are specialized fibers with sensory endings rather than satellite cells.

cards.q: Which training program raises the oxidative enzyme activity of a muscle the most?
cards.a: Endurance training.
options: Heavy resistance training
Endurance training
A single maximal effort repeated once a week
Complete rest, which conserves enzyme protein
cards.explanation: Repeated prolonged submaximal activity signals the fiber to build more mitochondria and more of the enzymes inside them, which is the core endurance adaptation. Heavy resistance training builds contractile protein rather than oxidative capacity. A single weekly maximal effort provides too little total aerobic work to drive mitochondrial biogenesis. Rest lowers oxidative enzyme activity rather than conserving it, because the stimulus that maintains the machinery is removed.

cards.q: How does atrophy after cutting the motor nerve compare with atrophy from immobilizing a limb with an intact nerve?
cards.a: Denervation atrophy is faster and more severe.
options: Denervation atrophy is slower and milder
Denervation atrophy is faster and more severe
The two produce identical rates and degrees of atrophy
Denervation causes hypertrophy rather than atrophy
cards.explanation: A denervated muscle loses both mechanical loading and the trophic influence of its motor neuron, so it wastes faster and further than a muscle that is merely unloaded but still innervated. Losing two influences cannot be milder than losing one. The two situations are therefore not equivalent, which is why nerve injury carries a worse prognosis for muscle mass. Denervation never produces growth; the fibers shrink and, over long periods, can be replaced by connective tissue and fat.

cards.q: After twelve weeks of heavy resistance training, fiber cross sectional area has risen by 25 percent while the number of capillaries per fiber is unchanged. Predict what happens to capillary density expressed per unit of fiber area.
cards.a: It falls, because the same number of capillaries now serves a larger fiber.
options: It falls, because the same number of capillaries now serves a larger fiber
It rises, because larger fibers always attract new capillaries
It is unchanged, because capillary number and fiber size always change together
It falls, because resistance training destroys capillaries
cards.explanation: Density is a ratio, so holding the numerator fixed while the denominator grows by a quarter must lower the value, which is one reason pure strength training does not improve endurance. Capillary growth does occur with some programs, but the stem states capillary number per fiber did not change. Capillary number and fiber size are regulated by different signals and often move independently. Nothing in resistance training destroys capillaries; the ratio falls purely because the fibers grew.

cards.q: A leg is immobilized in a cast for six weeks. Predict what happens to fiber cross sectional area and to mitochondrial content.
cards.a: Both decrease.
options: Both decrease
Cross sectional area decreases and mitochondrial content increases
Cross sectional area increases and mitochondrial content decreases
Both are unchanged, because the nerve supply remains intact
cards.explanation: Disuse removes both the mechanical load that maintains contractile protein and the metabolic demand that maintains mitochondria, so the fiber loses on both fronts. Mitochondria do not increase when demand disappears. Cross sectional area cannot grow without loading, so the third option has the direction backward. An intact nerve slows the loss compared with denervation, but it does not prevent it.

cards.q: A previously sedentary person trains for a marathon over six months. Predict the change in mitochondrial content and in maximal oxygen consumption.
cards.a: Both increase.
options: Mitochondrial content increases and maximal oxygen consumption is unchanged
Both increase
Mitochondrial content is unchanged and maximal oxygen consumption increases
Both decrease as the fibers become smaller and more efficient
cards.explanation: Endurance training raises mitochondrial content in the trained muscle and improves cardiac output and oxygen extraction, so both the local and the whole body measures rise together. Mitochondrial gains without any change in maximal oxygen consumption would be unusual in a previously sedentary person, since central adaptations occur as well. Maximal oxygen consumption rarely improves without the peripheral changes that let muscle use the delivered oxygen. Neither measure falls with training, even though fiber diameter may drop slightly.

cards.q: Two programs are compared over twelve weeks: heavy low repetition lifting and long slow distance running. Which program produces the larger increase in maximal voluntary force?
cards.a: The lifting program, because it drives hypertrophy and improved neural drive.
options: The running program, because it improves oxygen delivery to the fibers
The running program, because slow fibers generate the most force per unit area
The lifting program, because it drives hypertrophy and improved neural drive
Neither, because maximal force is fixed by fiber type and cannot be trained
cards.explanation: Maximal force scales with contractile protein and with how completely the nervous system can recruit and drive the motor units, and heavy lifting improves both. Better oxygen delivery raises endurance rather than peak force. Slow fibers do not produce more force per unit area than fast fibers, and they are the smaller fibers besides. Maximal force is highly trainable, which is why strength programs work in the first place.

cards.q: A patient is on strict bed rest for four weeks. Predict the change in fatigue resistance when normal activity resumes.
cards.a: Fatigue resistance is reduced, because mitochondrial content and capillary supply have fallen.
options: Fatigue resistance is improved, because the muscle has been fully rested
Fatigue resistance is unchanged, because it depends only on fiber type
Fatigue resistance is reduced, because the number of motor units has fallen
Fatigue resistance is reduced, because mitochondrial content and capillary supply have fallen
cards.explanation: Bed rest removes the activity that maintains oxidative capacity, so mitochondria and capillaries regress and the muscle tires quickly on return to activity. Rest of this length is deconditioning rather than recovery. Fiber type composition is only part of the picture, and the oxidative machinery within a given fiber type is itself trainable. Motor unit number is set by the number of motor neurons, which bed rest does not reduce.

cards.q: Predict the fiber type shift produced by several months of endurance training.
cards.a: A shift from fast glycolytic toward fast oxidative glycolytic properties.
options: A shift from slow oxidative toward fast glycolytic properties
A shift from fast oxidative glycolytic toward fast glycolytic properties
A shift from fast glycolytic toward fast oxidative glycolytic properties
No shift at all, because fiber type is fixed by genetics
cards.explanation: Chronic aerobic activity pushes fibers toward the oxidative end of the spectrum, so fast glycolytic fibers acquire more mitochondria and capillaries and take on fast oxidative glycolytic properties. Shifting toward the glycolytic end is what disuse and sprint style training encourage, not endurance work. Fiber type has a strong genetic component but is clearly modifiable by chronic activity pattern, as cross innervation and training studies both show.

cards.q: Biopsies before and after a twelve week program show fiber cross sectional area up 22 percent, capillaries per fiber unchanged, and mitochondrial volume density down 8 percent. Which program was most likely performed?
cards.a: Heavy resistance training.
options: Endurance cycling five days a week
Heavy resistance training
Six weeks of limb immobilization followed by six weeks of walking
Complete bed rest
cards.explanation: Growth in fiber area with no capillary gain and a diluted mitochondrial density is the classic hypertrophy signature, since new myofibrillar protein expands the fiber around a fixed complement of mitochondria and capillaries. Endurance cycling would raise mitochondrial density and capillary number while leaving area roughly flat. Immobilization followed by walking would at best return the fiber to baseline, not add 22 percent. Bed rest would shrink the fiber.

cards.q: An astronaut spends six months in microgravity with limited exercise. Predict what happens to postural muscle fiber size, capillary supply, and oxidative capacity, and name the main driver.
cards.a: All three decrease, driven by the loss of chronic mechanical loading and activity.
options: Fiber size decreases while capillary supply and oxidative capacity increase, driven by fluid shifts
All three increase, driven by the exercise countermeasures used in flight
All three are unchanged, because muscle adapts only to gravity over years rather than months
All three decrease, driven by the loss of chronic mechanical loading and activity
cards.explanation: Antigravity muscles such as the soleus lose their principal stimulus in microgravity, so contractile protein, capillary supply, and mitochondrial content all regress, much as they do with bed rest on Earth. Capillary and oxidative gains would require increased activity, which is exactly what is missing. Countermeasure exercise slows the loss but does not reverse it into net gain in this scenario. Detectable atrophy appears within weeks, not years.

cards.q: A coach must choose between two twelve week programs for a client whose goals are a higher one repetition maximum squat and a faster 5 kilometer run time. Which prediction about the two programs is best supported by muscle plasticity?
cards.a: Lifting raises the squat more and running lowers the run time more, since the adaptations are separate.
options: Endurance running will improve both, because aerobic fitness is the foundation of every kind of performance
Heavy lifting will improve both, because a stronger muscle is automatically more fatigue resistant
Either program will improve both equally, because all training raises total muscle protein
Lifting raises the squat more and running lowers the run time more, since the adaptations are separate
cards.explanation: Hypertrophy and neural adaptations drive maximal force, while mitochondrial and capillary adaptations drive endurance, and each is produced mainly by its own kind of loading, so goals that pull in different directions need different programs. Aerobic training does not build the contractile mass a heavy squat requires. A larger fiber is not automatically more fatigue resistant, because hypertrophy dilutes mitochondrial density. Training adaptations are specific to the stimulus rather than a generic increase in protein.

cards.q: A trained endurance athlete stops training entirely. Mitochondrial content falls measurably within about two weeks, while maximal oxygen consumption declines more slowly over several weeks. What does this difference in time course indicate?
cards.a: Local muscle adaptations regress faster than central cardiovascular ones.
options: Central cardiovascular adaptations regress faster than the local adaptations inside the muscle
Local muscle adaptations regress faster than central cardiovascular ones
Mitochondrial content and maximal oxygen consumption are unrelated measurements
The measurements conflict, so one of them must be in error
cards.explanation: Mitochondrial protein turns over quickly and depends on frequent activity to be maintained, while blood volume, cardiac dimensions, and capillary structure change more slowly, so the peripheral machinery is lost first during detraining. The reverse ordering does not match the observed timescales. The two measures are tightly linked, since delivered oxygen must be used by mitochondria to appear in the whole body value. Different rates of change in linked variables are ordinary physiology rather than a measurement error.

cards.q: What does a surface electromyogram record?
cards.a: The summed electrical activity of the fibers under the electrodes.
options: The force the muscle is producing at the tendon
The action potentials traveling down the motor nerve to the muscle
The concentration of Ca2+ released inside the fibers
The summed electrical activity of the fibers under the electrodes
cards.explanation: Surface EMG picks up the electrical field created by many muscle fiber action potentials occurring under the skin electrodes, which is why its amplitude reflects how much muscle is electrically active. Force is measured separately by a dynamometer, and the relationship between the two signals is exactly what the lab examines. Motor nerve action potentials are far too small and too deep to register on surface electrodes. Intracellular Ca2+ cannot be detected from the skin surface at all.

cards.q: What does a hand dynamometer measure in the grip fatigue lab?
cards.a: The force the hand exerts during a grip.
options: The electrical activity of the forearm flexors
The force the hand exerts during a grip
The rate of ATP use in the forearm muscles
The number of motor units recruited in the forearm
cards.explanation: A dynamometer is a force transducer, so it reports how hard the hand squeezes, usually in kilograms or newtons. Electrical activity is what the EMG electrodes report, and pairing the two signals is the point of the experiment. ATP use is not measured directly in this lab. Motor unit number can only be inferred, and then only indirectly, from the EMG signal rather than from the force record.

cards.q: Surface EMG amplitude increases mainly because of which two changes in the muscle?
cards.a: More motor units are recruited and active units fire faster.
options: The fibers shorten faster and the tendon stretches further
More motor units are recruited and active units fire faster
More Ca2+ is released per action potential and troponin binds more of it
The muscle warms up and its electrical resistance falls
cards.explanation: EMG amplitude is a summed electrical signal, so it grows when more fibers are firing and when each active unit fires more often, which are the same two mechanisms the nervous system uses to increase force. Shortening velocity and tendon stretch are mechanical events and do not add electrical signal. Ca2+ release and troponin binding occur after the action potential and are not detected by the electrodes. Warming does change tissue impedance slightly, but that is a minor effect compared with recruitment and rate coding.

cards.q: Grip force in this lab is most commonly reported in which units?
cards.a: Kilograms or newtons.
options: Kilograms or newtons
Millivolts or microvolts
Milliseconds
Hertz
cards.explanation: Force is force, so the dynamometer reads in kilograms of force or in newtons. Millivolts and microvolts are the units of the EMG voltage signal, which is recorded on a separate channel. Milliseconds measure the duration of events such as the latent period. Hertz measures stimulus or firing frequency rather than force.

cards.q: Why are surface EMG electrodes placed over the belly of the muscle rather than over the tendon?
cards.a: The belly contains the contractile fibers that generate the electrical signal.
options: The tendon carries a larger signal that would saturate the amplifier
The tendon is where the motor nerve enters the muscle
The belly contains the contractile fibers that generate the electrical signal
Skin over the tendon has a lower electrical resistance
cards.explanation: Only muscle fibers generate action potentials, and they are concentrated in the belly, so that is where the recorded signal is largest and most representative. Tendon is collagen and is electrically silent, so it produces a smaller signal, not a larger one. The motor nerve typically enters near the middle of the muscle belly, not at the tendon. Skin impedance depends on preparation of the skin rather than on what lies beneath it.

cards.q: What is a maximal voluntary contraction, usually abbreviated MVC?
cards.a: The greatest force a subject can produce voluntarily against the transducer.
options: The force produced when the motor nerve is stimulated supramaximally
The greatest force a subject can produce voluntarily against the transducer
The force at which the EMG signal first becomes detectable
The force a subject can hold for at least five minutes
cards.explanation: MVC is a voluntary measure and serves as the reference against which submaximal target forces such as 30 percent or 60 percent are set. Force from supramaximal nerve stimulation is an evoked measure and can exceed MVC when central fatigue is present. The point where EMG first appears is closer to a threshold of activation than to a maximum. A force sustainable for five minutes is an endurance measure, far below MVC.

cards.q: Why is a raw surface EMG signal usually rectified and then integrated or averaged before analysis?
cards.a: The raw signal swings above and below zero, so a plain average would cancel to near zero.
options: Rectification converts the electrical signal into units of force
The raw signal swings above and below zero, so a plain average would cancel to near zero
Integration removes the contribution of deeper motor units
Rectification eliminates the electromechanical delay between the EMG signal and the force record
cards.explanation: Motor unit potentials are biphasic, so the raw trace has positive and negative excursions that cancel; taking absolute values first, then smoothing, gives an amplitude measure that tracks activation. Rectification does not convert volts to newtons, and the two signals stay on separate calibrated channels. Integration smooths the signal without selecting for depth. The electromechanical delay between EMG and force is a physiological interval and is not removed by processing.

cards.q: During a sustained fatiguing contraction, how does the median frequency of the EMG power spectrum change?
cards.a: It shifts downward.
options: It shifts upward
It shifts downward
It stays constant while amplitude falls
It becomes undetectable once fatigue begins
cards.explanation: Fatigue slows muscle fiber conduction velocity, which stretches out each motor unit action potential and shifts the power spectrum toward lower frequencies, making the downward shift a standard objective marker of peripheral fatigue. An upward shift is what you would see with faster conduction, the opposite condition. Median frequency changes reliably during fatigue rather than staying fixed. The signal remains perfectly detectable, which is why the shift can be measured at all.

cards.q: A subject holds a steady 30 percent of maximum grip force for three minutes. Force stays on target, but EMG amplitude climbs throughout. What explains this?
cards.a: More motor units are recruited and firing rates rise to replace fatiguing units.
options: The fatiguing fibers generate larger action potentials as they tire
The dynamometer is drifting out of calibration during the hold
The skin impedance under the electrodes falls steadily as the subject sweats during the hold
More motor units are recruited and firing rates rise to replace fatiguing units
cards.explanation: As early recruited units fatigue and contribute less force, the nervous system must recruit more units and drive them faster to keep force on target, and all that extra electrical activity shows up as rising EMG amplitude. Individual fiber action potentials actually get slower and smaller with fatigue, not larger. A drifting transducer would show as a drifting force record, which the stem says is steady. Falling skin impedance from sweat can add a small amount, but it cannot account for a progressive rise across three minutes of constant force.

cards.q: A subject squeezes at maximum effort continuously for 60 seconds. Force falls steadily and EMG amplitude also falls. How should this be interpreted?
cards.a: Nothing is left in reserve, so fatigue lowers force and activation together.
options: The muscle is relaxing voluntarily, since a fall in EMG can only mean the subject stopped trying
The electrodes have detached, since a fatiguing muscle always shows rising EMG
Nothing is left in reserve, so fatigue lowers force and activation together
Force and EMG always fall together, so the recording contains no information about fatigue
cards.explanation: During a maximal effort everything is already recruited from the start, so there is no reserve to call on, and as fibers fatigue and central drive wanes both the force and the electrical signal decline together. Falling EMG during a maximal effort is expected and does not by itself prove the subject stopped trying. Rising EMG is the signature of a submaximal hold, not of every fatiguing contraction, so detached electrodes are not the only explanation. The joint decline is exactly the informative finding that distinguishes a maximal protocol from a submaximal one.

cards.q: Two subjects produce identical grip force, but one has considerably more subcutaneous fat over the forearm. Predict the effect on recorded surface EMG amplitude.
cards.a: The subject with more subcutaneous fat shows a smaller recorded amplitude for the same force.
options: The subject with more subcutaneous fat shows a smaller recorded amplitude for the same force
The subject with more subcutaneous fat shows a larger recorded amplitude for the same force
The amplitudes are identical, because EMG amplitude depends only on the force produced
The amplitudes are identical, because rectification corrects for tissue thickness
cards.explanation: Fat is a poor conductor and increases the distance from the active fibers to the electrodes, so the recorded signal is attenuated even though the muscle is working just as hard. Extra tissue between source and electrode cannot amplify a signal. Amplitude therefore depends on recording conditions as well as on force, which is why EMG values are compared within a subject rather than between subjects. Rectification changes the shape of the signal but does not restore lost amplitude.

cards.q: A subject holds 60 percent of maximum grip force in one trial and 30 percent in another, each to the point of failure. Predict the relative endurance times and the reason.
cards.a: The 30 percent hold lasts much longer, because fewer motor units are needed and blood flow is less obstructed.
options: The 60 percent hold lasts longer, because higher force recruits more fatigue resistant fibers
The two holds last about the same time, because both end in complete fatigue
The 30 percent hold lasts longer, because low force contractions use no ATP
The 30 percent hold lasts much longer, because fewer motor units are needed and blood flow is less obstructed
cards.explanation: Lower target force calls on fewer and mostly oxidative motor units and compresses the vessels within the muscle less, so oxygen keeps arriving and the hold can be sustained far longer. Higher force recruits fast fatigable units, not fatigue resistant ones, so it shortens endurance. Endurance time is steeply and inversely related to target force, so the two trials are not equivalent. Low force contractions certainly use ATP, just at a lower rate that oxidative metabolism can match.

cards.q: An EMG trace shows large, slow, irregular deflections that appear each time the subject shifts position in the chair, even when grip force is zero. What is the most likely source?
cards.a: Movement artifact from the electrodes and cables shifting on the skin.
options: Recruitment of additional motor units in the resting forearm
Cardiac electrical activity conducted to the forearm electrodes
The downward shift in median frequency that accompanies fatigue
Movement artifact from the electrodes and cables shifting on the skin
cards.explanation: Signals that are time locked to body movement rather than to force, and that persist when the muscle is at rest, are almost always mechanical artifact at the skin electrode interface. Motor unit recruitment would produce force, and the stem states force is zero. Cardiac signal appears as a small regular deflection at heart rate rather than as irregular movement locked deflections. A median frequency shift is a change in the spectrum of a genuine EMG signal and does not create deflections during rest.

cards.q: A subject doubles grip force from 20 percent to 40 percent of maximum. Predict what happens to the rectified EMG amplitude.
cards.a: It increases substantially, because both recruitment and firing rate rise.
options: It stays the same, because the same muscle is being used
It decreases, because higher force requires fewer but larger motor units
It increases substantially, because both recruitment and firing rate rise
It doubles exactly, because EMG amplitude and force are linearly proportional
cards.explanation: Producing more force requires activating more motor units and driving them at higher rates, and both changes add electrical activity, so amplitude rises clearly with force. Using the same muscle does not mean using the same amount of it. Higher force recruits additional large units on top of the small ones, rather than fewer units. The relationship is monotonic but not exactly proportional, since it depends on fiber depth, cancellation between overlapping potentials, and recording conditions.

cards.q: A right handed subject records a higher maximal grip force in the right hand than the left. What is the most reasonable physiological interpretation?
cards.a: The dominant forearm has slightly more muscle and better practiced neural drive.
options: The dominant forearm has slightly more muscle and better practiced neural drive
The dominant forearm has a different fiber type composition determined at birth
The dominant forearm has more motor units, since motor units are added with use
The difference must be a calibration error, since both hands share the same nervous system
cards.explanation: Habitual use of the dominant hand produces modest hypertrophy and more effective recruitment, which together explain the usual difference of roughly 10 percent. Fiber type composition does differ between people, but it does not differ systematically between a person's two arms because of handedness. Motor unit number is fixed by the number of motor neurons and does not increase with use. A consistent, reproducible difference in the expected direction is a real finding rather than an artifact.

cards.q: During a two minute hold at 40 percent of maximum, grip force stays on target for 60 seconds while EMG amplitude rises 25 percent, and then force falls 30 percent over the next 60 seconds while EMG amplitude falls back toward its starting value. What is the best two step interpretation?
cards.a: Compensatory recruitment held force early, and once the reserve was gone both fell.
options: The muscle grew stronger for the first minute and then weaker for the second
The electrodes gradually detached, which explains both the rise and the later fall in amplitude
The subject increased effort for the first minute and then deliberately relaxed
Compensatory recruitment held force early, and once the reserve was gone both fell
cards.explanation: The rising EMG at constant force in the first minute is the nervous system recruiting extra units to replace fatiguing ones, and when no reserve remains, further fatigue plus declining central drive drop force and electrical activity together. Muscle cannot gain strength within a minute, so the first option misreads the rising signal. Detaching electrodes would produce a monotonic loss of signal, not a rise followed by a fall. Deliberate relaxation is possible but is not the physiologically expected pattern in a standardized hold to failure.

cards.q: After a fatiguing grip protocol and two minutes of rest, a subject's maximal force has recovered to 85 percent of the prefatigue value, but the EMG median frequency is still well below baseline. What does this combination indicate?
cards.a: Force recovery outpaces recovery of the fiber, so peripheral fatigue persists.
options: Recovery is complete and the residual frequency shift is an artifact of the rest period
Central fatigue has persisted while the peripheral component has fully resolved during the rest
Force recovery outpaces recovery of the fiber, so peripheral fatigue persists
The muscle has adapted to the protocol within two minutes, raising its fatigue resistance
cards.explanation: Median frequency tracks fiber conduction velocity, which depends on the ionic and metabolic state inside the fiber, and those take longer than two minutes to normalize even as gross force largely returns. A reproducible spectral shift is a measurement of a real state rather than an artifact. Persisting central fatigue would show as a force deficit recoverable by stimulation, and it would not explain a spectral shift, which is a peripheral marker. Training adaptations take weeks, not two minutes.

cards.q: A blood pressure cuff is inflated above systolic pressure on the upper arm and the subject then performs repeated grip contractions at 30 percent of maximum. Compared with the same protocol with free circulation, predict the force decline and the EMG amplitude behavior.
cards.a: Force falls much faster, and EMG amplitude rises steeply as the nervous system recruits harder to compensate.
options: Force falls much faster, and EMG amplitude falls immediately because the nerve is compressed
Force is maintained longer, because occlusion traps oxygenated blood in the forearm
Force falls much faster, and EMG amplitude rises steeply as the nervous system recruits harder to compensate
Force and EMG behave exactly as they do with free circulation, since 30 percent of maximum is a low target
cards.explanation: Cutting off arterial supply forces the working fibers into anaerobic metabolism and traps the byproducts, so peripheral fatigue develops rapidly, and the nervous system compensates by recruiting more units, which drives EMG amplitude up steeply. Nerve compression under a cuff takes many minutes and does not explain a fast force decline. Trapped blood is stripped of oxygen within seconds and cannot sustain the muscle. Low target forces are normally sustainable for minutes precisely because circulation keeps up, which is what the cuff removes.

cards.q: Two subjects hold 50 percent of their own maximum to failure. Subject 1 lasts 45 seconds with a rapid force decay; subject 2 lasts 140 seconds with a gradual decay. Assuming similar effort and technique, what does this suggest about their forearm muscle composition?
cards.a: Subject 2 likely has a greater proportion of oxidative fibers and a denser capillary supply.
options: Subject 2 likely has a greater proportion of fast glycolytic fibers
Subject 1 likely has more total motor units, allowing faster recruitment
The difference must reflect maximal strength, since a stronger subject always fatigues faster
Subject 2 likely has a greater proportion of oxidative fibers and a denser capillary supply
cards.explanation: Endurance at a fixed percentage of each subject's own maximum reflects the fatigue resistance of the fibers doing the work, so the longer holding subject probably carries more slow oxidative fibers with a better capillary supply. Fast glycolytic fibers fatigue quickly and would shorten the hold, not lengthen it. Motor unit number does not vary in a way that would explain a threefold endurance difference. Because each target is set as a percentage of the subject's own maximum, absolute strength has largely been normalized out.

cards.q: In a muscle stimulation experiment, what is the threshold stimulus?
cards.a: The smallest stimulus voltage that produces a measurable contraction.
options: The smallest stimulus voltage that activates every motor unit in the muscle
The stimulus frequency at which individual twitches begin to fuse
The stimulus voltage above which further increases damage the muscle
The smallest stimulus voltage that produces a measurable contraction
cards.explanation: Threshold is the voltage at which the first and most excitable motor units reach their firing threshold, so it is the lowest voltage that produces any tension at all. The voltage that activates every motor unit is the maximal stimulus, which is much higher. The frequency at which twitches begin to fuse is a frequency phenomenon, not a voltage one. Damaging voltages are a practical concern in a real preparation but are not what threshold means.

cards.q: What is the maximal stimulus in a muscle stimulation experiment?
cards.a: The lowest voltage that activates every motor unit, so force stops rising.
options: The highest voltage the stimulator can deliver
The lowest voltage that produces any detectable contraction in the muscle at all
The voltage that produces complete tetanus in a single stimulus
The lowest voltage that activates every motor unit, so force stops rising
cards.explanation: As voltage rises, progressively less excitable motor units are recruited, and once the last one is included, further voltage adds nothing, which defines the maximal stimulus. The stimulator's ceiling is a property of the equipment rather than of the muscle. The lowest voltage producing any contraction is threshold, at the other end of the recruitment range. Tetanus depends on stimulus frequency, and no single stimulus can produce it at any voltage.

cards.q: What are the three phases of a single muscle twitch as recorded on a tracing?
cards.a: Latent period, contraction phase, relaxation phase.
options: Latent period, contraction phase, relaxation phase
Threshold, summation, tetanus
Depolarization, repolarization, hyperpolarization
Recruitment, treppe, fatigue
cards.explanation: A twitch tracing starts with a latent period in which tension has not yet appeared, then a contraction phase as tension rises to peak, then a relaxation phase as tension returns to baseline. Threshold, summation, and tetanus describe how twitches respond to stimulus intensity and frequency rather than the shape of one twitch. Depolarization and repolarization are phases of the action potential, an electrical event that precedes the mechanical one. Recruitment, treppe, and fatigue are separate phenomena of repeated stimulation.

cards.q: What is happening during the latent period of a muscle twitch?
cards.a: Excitation contraction coupling is underway, but tension has not yet appeared.
options: Ca2+ is being pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
The muscle is relaxing from the tension developed during the previous stimulus
Excitation contraction coupling is underway, but tension has not yet appeared
The stimulator is charging before it delivers the pulse
cards.explanation: During the latent period the action potential spreads, the T tubules signal the sarcoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+ is released, and the series elastic elements begin to take up slack, all before measurable tension appears. Ca2+ reuptake happens later, during the relaxation phase. In a single twitch from rest there is no previous stimulus to relax from. The latent period is a property of the muscle, not of the stimulator's electronics.

cards.q: What is treppe, sometimes called the staircase effect?
cards.a: A progressive rise in twitch force over the first several identical stimuli.
options: A progressive rise in twitch force over the first several identical stimuli
The fusion of successive twitches into a smooth tetanus
The progressive fall in force during a sustained tetanus
The stepwise increase in whole muscle force as the stimulus voltage is raised
cards.explanation: When a rested muscle is stimulated repeatedly at a low frequency, the first several twitches get stronger even though the stimulus is unchanged, mainly because Ca2+ accumulates in the sarcoplasm and enzyme activity rises with warming. Fusion of twitches is summation leading to tetanus, which is a different phenomenon. Force falling during a sustained tetanus is fatigue. Stepwise increases with rising voltage are multiple motor unit recruitment.

cards.q: What produces incomplete or unfused tetanus?
cards.a: Stimuli arriving before full relaxation, so twitches summate but tension still ripples.
options: Stimuli arriving before full relaxation, so twitches summate but tension still ripples
Stimuli arriving after the muscle has fully relaxed, producing a train of separate twitches
A stimulus voltage between threshold and maximal, producing partial recruitment
Stimuli continuing after the muscle has begun to fatigue
cards.explanation: If the next stimulus arrives while some tension remains, the new twitch adds on top of it, and force climbs to a level higher than a single twitch while still showing a visible ripple. Stimuli spaced beyond full relaxation give a train of separate twitches, not tetanus. A submaximal voltage changes how many motor units contribute, not whether their twitches fuse. Fatigue causes force to fall during a stimulus train rather than producing the fused or unfused pattern.

cards.q: What defines complete or fused tetanus on a tracing?
cards.a: A smooth sustained plateau with no relaxation between stimuli.
options: A smooth sustained plateau with no relaxation between stimuli
A tension record showing distinct peaks separated by periods of partial relaxation
The maximal tension a single twitch can produce
A tension record that falls steadily throughout the stimulus train
cards.explanation: At high enough stimulus frequency there is no time for any relaxation between stimuli, so Ca2+ stays elevated and tension holds a smooth maximal plateau. Distinct peaks with partial relaxation describe unfused tetanus, one step below. A single twitch produces far less tension than tetanus, typically a third to a fifth as much. Steadily falling tension during a train is fatigue, not fusion.

cards.q: Between threshold and maximal voltage, why does whole muscle force increase as stimulus voltage is raised?
cards.a: Progressively more motor units are brought to threshold and contribute to the total force.
options: Progressively more motor units are brought to threshold and contribute to the total force
Each activated fiber produces a larger action potential at higher voltage
The frequency of stimulation rises with voltage
Ca2+ release per action potential rises with voltage
cards.explanation: Motor units differ in excitability, so raising voltage recruits additional units, and their individual contributions add up, which is called multiple motor unit summation. A muscle fiber action potential is all or none, so it does not get larger with a stronger stimulus. Voltage and frequency are set independently on the stimulator. The Ca2+ released per action potential is likewise fixed for a given fiber and does not scale with stimulus strength.

cards.q: A simulated muscle reaches its maximal stimulus at 4.0 V. Predict what happens to twitch force when the voltage is raised from 4.0 V to 8.0 V.
cards.a: Force stays the same, because every motor unit is already recruited.
options: Force doubles, because voltage doubled
Force rises modestly, because the remaining fibers fire more strongly
Force falls, because the higher voltage inactivates some fibers
Force stays the same, because every motor unit is already recruited
cards.explanation: Once the maximal stimulus is reached, there are no unrecruited motor units left to add, so extra voltage produces no extra force, which is exactly how the maximal stimulus is identified in the simulation. Force does not scale with voltage; it scales with how many units the voltage recruits. Fibers already firing cannot fire more strongly, because the action potential is all or none. Excess voltage would damage a real preparation, but in the simulation force simply plateaus.

cards.q: A muscle is stimulated at a maximal voltage, and the frequency is raised from 5 Hz to 20 Hz. Predict what happens to the tracing.
cards.a: Individual twitches begin to summate, so peak tension rises above single twitch tension.
options: Individual twitches begin to summate, so peak tension rises above single twitch tension
The tracing shows the same twitch height but four times as many twitches
Peak tension falls, because the muscle has less time to recover between stimuli
The muscle enters complete fused tetanus immediately at 20 Hz
cards.explanation: At 5 Hz the stimuli are 200 ms apart, long enough for full relaxation, but at 20 Hz they are 50 ms apart, so a new twitch begins before the previous one has decayed and the tensions add. Simply seeing more twitches of unchanged height would require the interval to still exceed the twitch duration. Tension rises rather than falls, since fatigue is not the dominant effect at this frequency early in a train. Complete fusion usually requires a higher frequency, so 20 Hz commonly gives unfused tetanus.

cards.q: In a simulation, the stimulus interval is set shorter than the muscle's relaxation time but long enough that a small dip in tension still occurs between stimuli. What will the tracing look like?
cards.a: An oscillating ripple riding on an elevated plateau, or unfused tetanus.
options: A series of identical separate twitches each returning fully to baseline
A perfectly smooth plateau with no oscillation
An oscillating ripple riding on an elevated plateau, or unfused tetanus
A single twitch followed by a flat baseline
cards.explanation: Partial relaxation between stimuli produces the characteristic ripple of unfused tetanus, with average tension well above single twitch level. Separate twitches returning to baseline require intervals longer than the twitch duration. A perfectly smooth plateau is complete tetanus, which needs a shorter interval than described. A single twitch would mean the stimulator delivered only one pulse.

cards.q: A stimulus of 0.2 V is delivered to a simulated muscle whose threshold is 0.8 V. Predict the result.
cards.a: No contraction, because no motor unit reaches threshold.
options: A small contraction, since some fibers always respond to any stimulus
A normal sized twitch, since muscle contraction is all or none
A delayed contraction, since subthreshold stimuli take longer to act
No contraction, because no motor unit reaches threshold
cards.explanation: Below threshold no motor axon is brought to firing level, so no fiber contracts and the tracing stays flat. Fibers do not respond partially to a subthreshold stimulus, since the axon either fires or it does not. The all or none rule applies to individual fibers, not to a whole muscle, and it does not mean any stimulus produces a full twitch. Subthreshold stimuli do not eventually produce a delayed contraction; they produce none at all.

cards.q: What intracellular condition must be maintained for a muscle to hold complete fused tetanus?
cards.a: Sarcoplasmic Ca2+ must stay elevated between successive stimuli.
options: Sarcoplasmic Ca2+ must return to its resting level between successive stimuli
The fiber must remain depolarized continuously without repolarizing
ATP must be depleted so that crossbridges stay attached
Sarcoplasmic Ca2+ must stay elevated between successive stimuli
cards.explanation: Rapid stimulation releases Ca2+ faster than the sarcoplasmic reticulum can reclaim it, so troponin stays saturated, crossbridges keep cycling, and tension holds a smooth plateau. If Ca2+ returned to resting level between stimuli the muscle would relax and the tetanus would break up. The fiber does repolarize between action potentials; it is the mechanical response, not the electrical one, that fuses. Depleted ATP would produce rigor and a failure to relax, which is not what tetanus is.

cards.q: A simulated muscle produces 10 g of tension in a single maximal twitch. What tension would you expect during complete tetanus of the same muscle?
cards.a: About 30 to 50 g.
options: About 10 g, since all motor units are already recruited in the maximal twitch
About 15 g, since summation adds only a small increment
About 200 g, since each stimulus in the train adds a full twitch of tension
About 30 to 50 g
cards.explanation: Tetanic tension typically runs three to five times single twitch tension, because sustained high Ca2+ keeps far more crossbridges attached than the brief Ca2+ transient of a single twitch allows. Recruitment is indeed maximal in both cases, which is exactly why the extra force must come from frequency rather than from more motor units. A 50 percent increase understates summation considerably. Tension does not accumulate without limit across a train; it plateaus once every available crossbridge is engaged.

cards.q: A simulated twitch lasts about 100 ms from stimulus to full relaxation. Roughly what minimum stimulus frequency is needed before twitches begin to summate?
cards.a: Just above 10 Hz, since a 100 ms twitch means stimuli must be closer than 100 ms apart.
options: Just above 1 Hz, since any repeated stimulus summates
Just above 100 Hz, since frequency must exceed the twitch duration in milliseconds
Just above 50 Hz, since fusion always requires 50 Hz or more
Just above 10 Hz, since a 100 ms twitch means stimuli must be closer than 100 ms apart
cards.explanation: A 100 ms twitch means one stimulus every 100 ms, or 10 Hz, lands just as the previous twitch ends, so anything faster than 10 Hz makes the twitches overlap and summate. At 1 Hz the stimuli are a full second apart, leaving 900 ms of quiet baseline between them. Treating 100 ms as 100 Hz confuses the interval with the frequency; those are reciprocals, not the same number. Around 50 Hz would give complete fusion in this muscle, which is well above the frequency at which summation merely begins.

cards.q: A voltage series is run on a simulated muscle: 0.2 V gives 0 g, 0.4 V gives 0 g, 0.6 V gives 3 g, 1.5 V gives 12 g, 3.0 V gives 21 g, 4.5 V gives 24 g, 6.0 V gives 24 g. What are the threshold and maximal stimulus voltages?
cards.a: Threshold 0.6 V and maximal stimulus 4.5 V.
options: Threshold 0.2 V and maximal stimulus 6.0 V
Threshold 0.6 V and maximal stimulus 4.5 V
Threshold 0.6 V and maximal stimulus 6.0 V
Threshold 0.4 V and maximal stimulus 3.0 V
cards.explanation: Threshold is the lowest voltage that produces any tension, which is 0.6 V here, and the maximal stimulus is the lowest voltage at which force stops rising, which is 4.5 V because 6.0 V adds nothing. Choosing 0.2 V as threshold ignores that it produced no contraction at all. Calling 6.0 V maximal misses that the plateau had already been reached one step earlier, and the maximal stimulus is defined as the lowest such voltage. At 3.0 V force is still climbing, so recruitment is incomplete there.

cards.q: A maximal voltage is held constant while frequency is stepped through 4 Hz, 12 Hz, 25 Hz, and 60 Hz. The tracings show separate twitches, small ripples on a raised baseline, larger ripples on a much higher baseline, and a smooth plateau. Which explanation of the progression is correct?
cards.a: Less time for Ca2+ reuptake at high frequency, so twitches summate until tension fuses.
options: Rising frequency recruits progressively more motor units until every unit is active
Rising frequency increases the Ca2+ released per action potential until saturation
Rising frequency shortens the latent period until the twitches merge
Less time for Ca2+ reuptake at high frequency, so twitches summate until tension fuses
cards.explanation: With voltage held at maximal, every motor unit is already firing, so the only variable left is how often, and closer spacing keeps sarcoplasmic Ca2+ high and lets mechanical responses add until the record fuses. Recruitment cannot explain the change, since the constant maximal voltage means recruitment is already complete. Ca2+ released per action potential is fixed for a given fiber and does not grow with frequency. The latent period is essentially constant and far too brief to account for fusion.

cards.q: A rested simulated muscle is stimulated at 1 Hz with an unchanging maximal voltage. Twitch force rises from 8 g to 11 g over the first ten stimuli, holds near 11 g for two minutes, and then declines to 6 g. Which pair of mechanisms accounts for the rise and the later fall?
cards.a: Treppe from accumulating Ca2+ and warming, followed by metabolic fatigue.
options: Recruitment of additional motor units, followed by loss of motor units from the stimulus train
Treppe from accumulating Ca2+ and warming, followed by metabolic fatigue
Increasing stimulus voltage delivered by the stimulator, followed by voltage decay
Progressive summation of twitches, followed by complete tetanus and then relaxation
cards.explanation: The early rise at fixed stimulus strength is treppe, driven by Ca2+ that has not been fully cleared between stimuli and by rising enzyme activity as the muscle warms, and the later decline is ordinary fatigue as byproducts build up. Recruitment cannot change, because the voltage is maximal and unchanging, and motor units are not lost during a stimulus train. The stem specifies that voltage is constant, so a drifting stimulator is excluded. At 1 Hz the twitches are a full second apart and never summate, so this is not a fusion phenomenon.

cards.q: A simulation parameter is changed so that the sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ pump works at half its normal rate, which roughly doubles the relaxation time of each twitch. Predict the effect on the stimulus frequency needed to produce complete tetanus.
cards.a: A lower frequency now produces complete tetanus, because each twitch takes longer to decay.
options: A higher frequency is now needed, because each twitch produces less tension
The fusion frequency is unchanged, because it depends only on stimulus voltage
Complete tetanus becomes impossible, because Ca2+ can no longer reach the required level
A lower frequency now produces complete tetanus, because each twitch takes longer to decay
cards.explanation: Fusion occurs when the next stimulus arrives before the previous twitch has relaxed, so a longer relaxation phase means the stimuli can be further apart and still overlap, which lowers the fusion frequency. A slower pump does not reduce peak twitch tension in a way that would demand faster stimulation. Fusion frequency depends on twitch duration, not on voltage, which controls recruitment instead. Slowing reuptake actually makes Ca2+ easier to keep elevated, so tetanus becomes easier rather than impossible.
